Its fleece is not, like a sheep's, composed of soft wool, but thin-haired and rougher than a wild goat's. Every year it bears triplets, and the teats of its udders are always full of milk. Its bleating resembles most the lowing of a tender calf, for diverse lands bear all things different.

div.head: 431.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Thief who found a Gold Sword
div.p: I BOTH love gold, and I shrink from hostile Ares.

div.head: 432.—THEOCRITUS
div.p: Ah! poor Thyrsis, what use crying out thy two eyes? The kid is gone, the little dear; it is gone to Hades, for the cruel wolf caught it in his claws. The dogs bay, but what use is that now when it is gone, and neither bone nor dust of it left?

div.head: 433.—BY THE SAME
div.p: By the Muses, wilt thou play something sweet to me on the double flute? and I will lift up my harp and begin a tune, and the herd Daphnis shall stand close by and make music with the breath of the wax-joined pipe. Standing there hard by, inside the cave shaggy with hanging greenery, let us bereave Pan the goat-mounter of sleep.

div.head: 434.—BY THE SAME
div.docAuthor: Prefixed to a collection of Theocritus' works
div.p: The Chian TheocritusAn orator and sophist of the fourth century B.C. 1 is another, but I, the Theocritus who wrote these poems, am one of the many Syracusans, the son of Praxagoras and noble Philinna. I admitted no verse that is other than genuine.

div.head: 435.—BY THE SAME
div.p: This bank pays citizen and foreigner alike. Withdraw what you deposited, the reckoning counters meeting their liabilitiesIt is, of course, the banker himself who πρὸς λόγον ἐρχεται, not his reckoning counters (or, as we should say, his books)..2 Let others find pretexts for not paying; Caicus pays money deposited with him on demand, even at night.

div.head: 436.—An Inscription from Syracuse
div.p: THE votive offerings to Apollo were old, but as for the base it is in one case twenty, in another seven, in another twelve, and in this last case two hundred years later; for so the figures work out when counted.

div.head: 437.—THEOCRITUS
div.p: GOATHERD, on turning the corner of that path where the oaks are, thou shalt find a newly carved image made of a fig-bough, three forked, with the bark still on, without ears, but able with its generative phallus to do the work of Aphrodite. Round it is a most holy hedge, and a perennial stream issuing from the rocks feeds on all sides abundance of laurel, myrtle, and sweet-scented cypress, round which curl the tendrils of the vine, mother of the grape. In spring the shrill song of the blackbirds echoes here with its varied notes, and the brown nightingales pour from their throats their honeyed voice in response. Sit here and pray to kind Priapus to make me fall out of love with Daphnis, and sacrifice at once to him a fine kid. But if he grants the prayer I will offer him in return three sacrifices. I will kill him a heifer, a shaggy billy-goat, and the stalled lamb I have. May the god be benevolent and grant it.

div.head: 438.—PHILIPPUS
div.p:
WHEN the burrowing ants, the army of the earth, nibbled at the rustic bee-keeper's sweet dainty, the
old man in anger set the jar in a dish of water, thinking that, being creatures of the land, they would not get to it. But they, setting up fresh stalks of straw against it, quickly found their way, without anyone to steer them, to the vessel. So their dear belly induced even these tiny creatures to migrate from earth to water, the very newest variety of boatmen.

div.head: 439.—CRINAGORAS
div.p: Once hairy crown, deserted shell of the eye, fabric of the tongueless mouth, feeble fence of the brain, relic of the unburied dead, set by the wayside to draw a tear from passers-by, thou liest there by the path near the tree-trunk, that looking on thee we may learn what profit there is in being thrifty of life.

div.head: 440.—MOSCHUS
div.p: Cypris cried loudly her lost son Love. "If any-one hath seen Love straying in the cross-roads, he is my fugitive child, and the informer shall be rewarded. The reward is a kiss from Cypris; and if you bring him, not a mere kiss, stranger, but something besides. The boy is easily recognisable; you could tell him among twenty. His complexion is not pale, but like to fire. His eyes are piercing and aflame. Evil is his heart, but sweet his speech, for what he has in his mind he speaks not. His voice is like honey, but if he grow wroth his spirit cannot be tamed. A cozener he is, never speaking the truth; a cunning child, and the games he plays are savage. Plenty of hair on his head, and he has

div.head: 441.—PALLADAS OF ALEXANDRIA
div.docAuthor: On a Statue of HeraclesThe statue had doubtless been cast down by the Christians. 1
div.p: I MARVELLED seeing at the cross-roads Jove's brazen son, once constantly invoked, now cast aside, and in wrath I said: “Averter of woes, offspring of three nights, thou, who never didst suffer defeat, art to-day laid low.” But at night the god stood by my bed smiling, and said: “Even though I am a god I have learnt to serve the times.”

div.head: 442.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p:
A FISHERMAN was toiling to catch fish when a wealthy girl, seeing him, felt the pangs of love.
She made him her husband, and he exchanged his poverty for a life boasting of every luxury. Fortune stood by smiling, and said to Cypris: "This is not your achievement, but mine."

div.head: 443.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.p: OPEN not the recesses of thy mind to Aphrodite, for light Love at once rebounds from a heart that is hardened. The nature of passion is insinuating; if one receives the tip of the flaming arrow, the whole of it penetrates. Flatter not thy mind with lascivious hope, for it attracts the spirit and fans the consuming fire.

div.head: 444.—ERATOSTHENES SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: FAIR are the treasures of virginity, but if it were observed by all it would put an end to life. Therefore live in lawful wedlock, and give a mortal to the world to replace thee; but avoid lechery.

div.head: 445.—JULIANUS OF EGYPT
div.p: GOLDEN Tetianus, the Emperor wished to send you again to the distressed cities which had need of you; but you preferred a peaceful life, keeping to your home and inheritance, and increasing the righteously acquired fortune of your house. For Justice, enthroned beside you, knows that you loathe to touch wealth won from those you rule.

div.head: 446.—BY THE SAME
div.p:
ALL the paths of life are pleasant. In the middle of the city there are fame and society; at home our
ALL the paths of life are pleasant. In the middle of the city there are fame and society; at home our griefs are hidden. The country has its delights, sea-voyages give profit, and foreign countries acquaintanceships. Marriage produces domestic concord, while the unmarried life is ever free from care. A child is his father's defence, while the childless are quit of fear. It is the virtue of youth to give us courage, that of hoary hairs to give us wisdom. Therefore be of good heart, and live and produce offspring.

div.head: 447.—BY THE SAME
div.p: A MOTHER, banishing the memory of her pangs, killed her son who abandoned the field after the death of his comrades. For Sparta distinguishes purity of race by warriors' bravery, not by children's birth.

div.head: 448.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: FISHERMEN from Arcadia, what have we? We left what we caught and carry what we did not catch.i.e. lice.

div.head: 449.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Love would say if he were in love
div.p: WHO is this that overcame fire by fire, who quenched a torch with a torch? Who drew another bow against mine? A new Love by my might contends on equal terms with Love.

div.head: 450.—PHILEMON
div.p: If the dead in truth had use of their senses, as some say, I would have hanged myself to see Euripides.

div.head: 451.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Philomela would say to her Sister Procne
div.p: Thy wicked husband shut me up, ill-fated that I am, alone in a deep cave, and took my maidenhead. An abominable present he made me on this my calamitous marriage, cutting off my tongue and quenching Greek speech in me.

div.head: 452.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Thy sister Philomela, Procne, wishes thee well if this be well-wishing. Let the robe tell thee the suffering of my heart which savage Tereus inflicted on meShe wove a robe and told her story to her sister by the voice of the κερκίς or weaving-comb..¹ Shutting me up, luckless maid, in the shepherd's fold, he deprived me first of virginity and next of speech.
div.note: She wove a robe and told her story to her sister by the voice of the κερκίς or weaving-comb.

div.head: 453.—MELEAGER
div.p: Zeus who dwellest in heaven, the ox itself, a suppliant at thy altar, lows, begging to be saved from death. Release the ploughherplougher, son of Cronos; for thou thyself, O king, didst become a bull to bear Europa across the sea.

div.head: 454.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Calliope would say to George
div.p: THIS man, not Zeus, is my true father.

div.head: 455.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Apollo would say about Homer
div.p: THE song is mine, but divine Homer wrote it down.

div.head: 456.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: If thou hast taught me to love a bull that roams over the mountains, teach me to low so that I may call my dear husband

div.head: 457.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Achilles would say if Agamemnon were wounded
div.p: THOU knowest now, Agamemnon, my man-destroying wrath; thou knowest how great is Hector's strength in hand-to-hand combat. For all have now perished owing to thy insult fraught with disaster, and a greater woe, worse than death, has come upon thee. Thou sufferest the evil and intolerable sorrow due to thy folly, who wast the defence in battle of all the Greeks.

div.head: 458.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Ulysses would say on landing in Ithaca
div.p: HAIL, Ithaca! After all my labours and the bitter woes of the sea, right glad am I to reach thy soil, in

div.head: 459.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Achilles would say on seeing Ulysses in HadesSee Od. xi. 467 seq.
div.p: Of a truth Odysseus is the most resourceful of men. Alive he looks on what it is not allowed to see, the infernal recesses and the bitter pains of the dead. How did he venture to leave the holy light? Did some necessity bring him here against his will? Odysseus never has his fill of cunning devices on earth, on the sea, and among the dead.

div.head: 460.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Achilles would have said when he saw the Armour lying before himSee Il. xix. 12 seq.
div.p: MOTHER, thou bringest to thy valiant son this armour, a glorious gift such as no man ever looked on. Now I know that Pallas arms my hand against Hector, and prepares disgrace and death for the Trojans.

div.head: 461.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Pyrrhus would say on entering Troy
div.p: THE labour of my noble father was not completed, but I have come, preparing slaughter for all the Trojans; for I glory more exceedingly in my valour, and my might is capable of destroying in battle King Priam and all that Achilles left alive. The warlike city of Troy will I sack, and my spear shall complete the ten years' labour of the Greeks.

div.head: 462.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Deidamia would say when Pyrrhus had sacked Troy
div.p: Thou hast made to cease all the heavy woe of my heart for the fate of thy father Achilles, whom mournful Troy slew. But thou hast sacked all Troy; and to the Greeks who were eager for it thou hast given the undying glory which the ten years of war could not accomplish for the whole host of the Danai.

div.head: 463.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Hector would say when he saw Achilles in the Armour
div.p: Athena in her wrath has again clothed the son of Peleus in immortal mail. Some worse woe shall befall the unhappy Trojans and Hector and his father, since the goddess gave this man this armour.

div.head: 464.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Paris would say when Menelaus was woundedSee Il. iv. 104.
div.p: Out on you all, ye craven Argives! Menelaus is dead now and gives me greater glory.

div.head: 465.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Althaea, entreating Meleager, would saySee Il. ix. 584 seq.
div.p: My son, thou forgettest thy family and heedest not thy country's fate. Thou hast cast aside thy strong sword, putting Oeneus and Calydon and her people to shame.

div.head: 466.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Alcestis would say when Admetus yoked a Lion and Boar to his ChariotPelias had promised his daughter Alcestis to whoever could do this. 1
div.p: GREAT deeds of valour crowned thy chariot, and with excellently composed wedding hymns men celebrate thy bride.

div.head: 467.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Peleus would say on hearing that Achilles absented himself from the Battle
div.p: YE peaks of Pelias, who nursed him, tell my son, whom Chiron taught to be first in battle, to cast off his wrath and fatal enmity to the Greeks.

div.head: 468.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Hera would say when Heracles was deified
div.p: THY father, Heracles, has well rewarded thy valiant toil, since labour can bring to men unsurpassable renown after an infinite round of labours.

div.head: 469.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: LABOUR and immense toil procured thee the favour of occupying a blessed seat that no man reached before thee.

div.head: 470.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Achilles would say to reconcile Ajax with Ulysses
div.p: IT is not permitted to nourish ill-will among the dead. Now thou hast escaped the sorrows of earth, love thy friend; for Odysseus did not sin against

div.head: 471.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: What Nestor would say on learning of Ulysses' return The good man has escaped the merciless sea, and after toil has reached his fatherland, and he must be my better, as he has become well acquainted with cities and customs and the minds of men.

div.head: 472.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: On Ulysses It was after much toil that long-suffering Odysseus came home; yet Odysseus, the sacker of cities, surely has great fame on land and sea among men of future times.

div.head: 473.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: What Agamemnon would say when Achilles was armed Beetling Ilion is fallen, and God has given it a prey to the Greeks now that Achilles has cast off his wrath and arms his murderous hands.

div.head: 474.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: What Idothea would say on seeing Helen in PharosAccording to the story followed by Euripides in his Helena, the real Helen was in Egypt during the Trojan war. 1 I pity thy beauty, since thou art the child of Zeus. For I see a god-nourished form, and verily thou wast the cause of the ten years' war between Greeks and Trojans. Where is the help of aegis-bearing Zeus thy father? But go soon on thy way, making, by the kindness of Idothea, a safe voyage home over the back of the cruel sea.

div.head: 475.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Helen would say on seeing the Combat between Paris and MenelausAccording to the story followed by Euripides in his Helena, the real Helen was in Egypt during the Trojan war.
div.p: Ye warlike kings of Europe and Asia, for both of you it stands upon a razor's edge, which of you long-suffering men shall take unhappy me to wife. Let Father Zeus decide, but without Aphrodite's help, lest another thief of wedded women steal me, a disgrace to Greece.

div.head: 476.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Hector would say when Patroclus could not lift the Spear of Achilles
div.p: Thy weakness has defrauded Hector, for thou bringest me defective spoils.

div.head: 477.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Thetis would say when Telephus was tripped up by the vineTelephus, tripped up by a vine-branch, was overtaken and slain by Achilles. Thetis here foretells the death of Achilles.
div.p: Vine, what shall I do when Daphnaean Apollo lays low my vine-branch by the arrow of Alexander?
div.note: Telephus, tripped up by a vine-branch, was overtaken and slain by Achilles. Thetis here foretells the death of Achilles.

div.head: 478.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Priam would say when Helen advised the Greeks how to take Troy
div.p: Splendid is the gift thou offerest thy country.

div.head: 479.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Perseus would say after slaying the Monster, when Andromeda refused him
div.p: The cruel fetters of the rock have turned thy heart to stone, and now let the eye of Medusa turn thy body, too, to stone.

div.head: 480.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: What Hippodamia would say after the Death of Oenomaus if Pelops refused to marry her
div.p: Hippodamia. Thou turnest thy back on me now thou hast liberty to enjoy me. Pelops. Yea, for Love does not go hand in hand with such liberty. Love walks in another path.

div.head: 481.—JULIANUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.docAuthor: (When he came too late to lecture)
div.p: Both evening sleep and morning sleep overcame me, the latter having been too heavy and the former not having invited me. Let morning sleep begone and evening sleep come in kindly wise, knowing the just number of hours.

div.head: 482.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: WE Mortals of no account, even if we perform great deeds, do not survive long in the memory of anyone; but as for the great, if they do nothing, if they only breathe, as the Libyan said, it is engraved in adamant. For instance Zeno, the lord and emperor of our city, while in the middle of a game played with the capricious dice, found himself in this complicated position: when of the white men who were on their way back, the sixth line contained seven, the ninth one, and the tenth and summus two each, while the line after the summus had two, and the last piece was on the divus. Black had two on the eighth line, and as many on the eleventh; on the twelfth were two, and one on the thirteenth. There were two on Antigonus and also on the fifteenth and eighteenth, and the fourth line from the last (the twentieth) also had two. It was the king's turn to play for White, and not seeing the trap in store for him, he cast the three dice from the wooden box with its hidden ladder, and threw two, six, and five, so that at once he had eight single pieces in all which had formerly been next others (?). Avoid backgammonby the break-up of the three pairs, the single on the "divus" for some reason not being moved forward.,¹ as the king himself did not escape from its blind chance.

div.head: 483.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: On a Child who was poisoned by Peach= Persicum malum. Kernels From the murderous Persians Perseus brought back a murderous fruit which caused the death of Theognostus' child.

div.head: 484.—PALLADAS
div.p: ODYSSEUS once, when sailing on the sea, received as a gift a bag of winds—a very valuable thing. But this my Aeolus of the windy heart sends me a fowl stuffed with wind. You send me winged winds, my friend, yes wind, and I can't eat compressed air.

div.head: 485.—HELIODORUS
div.p: I SING Thetis, golden-haired Thetis, the immortal daughter of the sea-god Nereus, who by the counsel of Zeus wedded Peleus, the glory of the sea, our Aphrodite, her who bore from her womb the raging spearman, the Ares of war, the lightning of Greece, divine Achilles, whose glory reaches to heaven. By him Pyrrha bore Neoptolemus, the sacker of Troy and saviour of Greece. Be gracious unto us, blessed hero Neoptolemus, now lying in Delphian earth; receive favourably this sacrifice and ward off all fear from our city. Thetis I sing, golden-haired Thetis.

div.head: 486.—PALLADAS
div.p: WHEN my slave untied the paunch= Persicum malum. 1 you sent me, after tying it up yourself, he found it to be a bellows full of air.

div.head: 487.—BY THE SAME
div.p: You served me the food of fig-fattened pigs from Cyprus, dry and thirst-provoking. But when you find me sufficiently fig-fattened, either kill me at once or quench my thirst with Cyprian wine.

div.head: 488.—TRYPHO
div.p: TERRES,TERPES,A sort of haggis. harping beautifully at the Carneian feast of tabernacles, died . . . among the Lacedaemonians, not wounded by a sword or a missile, but by a fig on the lips. Alas! Death is never at a loss for occasions.

div.head: 489.—PALLADAS
div.p: A GRAMMARIAN'S daughter, having known a man, gave birth to a child which was masculine, feminine, and neuter.

div.head: 490.—HELIODORUS
div.p: WHEN wearing the stone Pantarbes (Fear-all), fear not the force of fire. The unexpectedi.e. the paradox that the stone is called "Fear-all," and yet fears not fire. 3 is easy for the Fates.

div.head: 491.—THEON
div.docAuthor: A Monostichon on the Days of the Week
div.p: JOVE, Mars, Venus, Moon, Saturn, Sun, Mercury.

div.head: 492.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Together lay shield and sword, arrows, cuirass, helmet, horse.

div.head: 493.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Shield, bow and arrows, helmet, sword, strong spear.

div.head: 494.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Arrow, bow, shield, helmet, spear, sword, cuirass.

div.head: 495.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Dwellers in Greece, noble chieftains, place no trust any longer in perfidious women. A woman overcame me, whom my foe Hector slew not.

div.head: 496.—ATHENAEUS
div.p: Hail! ye who are learned in the Stoic lore, ye whose holy pages contain the very best of doctrines, that virtue is the soul's only good. This is the only doctrine that saves the lives and cities of men. But indulgence of the flesh, an end dear to others, is only approved by one of all Mnemosyne's daughters.1 i.e. Erato.

div.head: 497.—CRATES
div.p: Hunger puts an end to love, or if not hunger, time. But if neither of these put out the fire, the only cure left for you is to hang yourself.

div.head: 498.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: BURY not the unburied; leave him to be the prey of dogs. Earth, the mother of all, will not receive the man who defiles the bed of his mother.

div.head: 499.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: GREY Time goes along in silence, but as he creeps by he steals the voices of speaking men. Himself unseen, he makes the seen unseen and brings the unseen to light. O undetermined end of the life of men who day by day advance towards the dark!

div.head: 500.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: No longer call the living heirs, but call the dead heirs. The dead are now heirs, and gain a great inheritance, departure from this wretched life.

div.head: 501.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE dead used to leave the city alive behind them, but we living now carry the city to her grave.

div.head: 502.—PALLADAS
div.p: I REQUIRE “conditum.”Wine spiced with honey and pepper. Where did “conditum” get its name from? for it is alien to the Greek tongue. If it is a Latin word you will know, who are such a good Latin scholar. Prepare it for me, then, for the malady of the stomach from which I suffer requires this drink, I am told.

div.head: 503.—BY THE SAME
div.p: I was not wrong in saying that there is a divine virtue in dizyphiAn unknown word, but possibly another form of ζίζυφον, the fruit of the jujube-tree..¹ The other day at least I applied a dizyphos to one suffering from a chronic quartan ague, and he became at once as fit as a dog-tick.

div.head: 504.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: CALLIOPE discovered the art of heroic verse; Clio the sweet music of the lyre which accompanies the dance; Euterpe the sonorous voice of the tragic chorus; Melpomene found for mortals the honey-toned barbitos, and charming Terpsichore gave us the artful flute; Erato invented cheering hymns to the gods; learned Polymnia the joys of the dance; Urania discovered the pole and the dance of the stars of heaven, and Thalia the plots and good moral teaching of comedy.

div.head: 505.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
THE painter never saw Terpsichore, but owing to his art the image deceives our eyes by its truth.
If, my friend, you ever hear the lyre that cheers the heart, admire Erato, who possesses such skill.
Euterpe shrills on perforated reeds, scattering on them and forcing through them the spirit of the skilled bee.
div.note: This refers to pantomime or, as we should now call it, "ballet."

div.head: 506.—PLATO
div.p: SOME say the Muses are nine, but how carelessly! Look at the tenth, Sappho from Lesbos.

div.head: 507.—CALLIMACHUS
div.p: THE rhythm and the manner are Hesiod's. He of Soli took as a model not the worst of poets, but, I am afraid, the most honeyed of his verses.It is difficult to see the point, but I do not venture to adopt Toup's μὴ <οὐ>, "not the most honeyed." The reference is to Hesiod, Works and Days, 383 seq. Hail! delicate phrases, the monument of Aratus' sleepless nights.

div.head: 508.—PALLADAS
div.p: If one wishes to enjoy a happy day, meeting you makes his day a good one; but if one wishes the contrary, not meeting you makes it a bad one.

div.head: 509.—LYSISTRATUS THE SEER
div.p: The women of Colias shall cook with oarsFrom Herodotus, viii. 96. Colias was near Salamis, and the prophecy is said to have been made long before the battle..¹

div.head: 510.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Critonianus married me, Solon begat me, my name was MelineMeltine, I was moulded by the hands of my husbandCritonianus was a sculptor..²

div.head: 511.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Asclepios ordered me in his kindness to adorn his grey locks with gold, and I gladly did it, since he deemed this service on my part to be pleasing to himA dedication to Aesculapius after a cure..³

div.head: 512.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Teacher of the ruler of Rome, be gracious to me, accepting kindly the mysteries of the book of Protus, the deep words revealed by the pen of PhiloponusProtus appears to be author, Philoponus the scribe of the book, but all is mysterious..⁴

div.head: 513.—CRINAGORAS
div.p: Thou didst excel in the many dramas that Menander, with one of the Muses or one of the Graces, wrote.

div.head: 514.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I AM the god who is always chanted in the chambers of brides, and Menis, the comic actor, polished me well for the wedding of newly-married Procilla, and sent me with this prayer: “Go, Hymenaeus, in friendly wise, to both bride and bridegroom.”

div.head: 515.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE Gracecp. v. 146.s are three, and thou art one born for these three, that the Graces may have a Grace.¹

div.head: 516.—CRINAGORAS
div.p: “LET every man ply his own trade,” indeed. Under the high Alps the shock-headed robbers, when they have a job in hand, thus avoid the watch-dogs. They grease themselves thickly with kidney-fat to deceive the dogs’ keen scent. It is more ready in devising evil than good, the Ligurian mindIn the year 27 B.C. Crinagoras accompanied Augustus on his journey to Spain, passing through Liguria..²

div.head: 517.—ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA
div.p: ORPHEUS charmed beasts and thou charmest Orpheus. Phoebus vanquished the PhrygianMarsyas.,³ but he yields to thee when thou playest, Glaphyrus—the name= refined. suits both thy art and thy person. Athena would never have thrown the flute awayAthena invented the flute, but threw it away in disgust as playing it disfigured her. had she made such music as thou, master of varied delight. Sleep himself, lying in Pasithea’s arms, would awake if he heard thee.

div.head: 518.—ALCAEUS OF MESSENE
div.p: HEIGHTEN thy walls, Olympian Zeus; all is accessible to Philip: shut the brazen gates of the gods. Earth and sea lie vanquished under Philip's sceptre: there remains the road to OlympusThe epigram is of course ironical. Alcaeus, as the next epigram shows, was the bitter enemy of King Philip V..¹

div.head: 519.—BY THE SAME
div.docAuthor: (Addressed to King Philip, son of Demetrius)
div.p: I DRINK, Bacchus, I drink; yes, deeper than the Cyclops drunk when he had filled his belly with the flesh of men; would I could dash out the brains of my foe and drain Philip's skull to the dregs, Philip who tastes of the blood of his friends as he carouses, pouring poison into the winePhilip is said to have poisoned Aratus, among others, in this manner..²

div.head: 520.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On Alcaeus (probably by his enemy King Philip)
div.p: THIS is the tomb of Alcaeus who was killed by the broad-leaved daughter of earth, the radish, punisher of adulterers.

div.head: 521.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: No little fame, Sappho, did Fate grant thee on the day thou didst first see the sun. For we consented that thy utterances should be immortal, and the Father of all, the Thunderer, approved. All men shall sing thee, and thou shalt not lack glorious report.

div.head: 522.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Iliad, thou great work, and Odyssey, chaste poem, that hast made Ithaca Troy's equal, make me, the old man, grow in eternal youth; for from your lips flows the Siren song of Homer.

div.head: 523.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Calliope, eloquent goddess of Helicon the pasture of bees, bear me a second Homer, since a second Achilles has come.

div.head: 524.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: A Hymn to Dionysus (containing his Epithets in Alphabetical Order)
div.p:
Let us chant the king who loves the call of EuhocEuhoe, the King Eiraphiotes,The meaning of this epithet is quite unknown. Tender-haired, rustic, much besung, fair of form, Boeotian, Bromius, reveller, with vine-leaves in his hair, Merry, productive, slayer of giants, the laughterlaugher, Son of Zeus, twice-born, son of the Dithyramb, Dionysus, Euius, with lovely locks, rich in vines, awakerawakener of revels, Jealous, very wrathful, envious, bestower of envy, Gentle, sweet drinker, sweet-voiced, cozener, Thracian, thyrsus-bearing, boon-companion, lion-hearted, Slayer of Indians, desirable, twiner of violets, hierophant, Reveller, horned, ivy-crowned, noisy,
Lydian, lord of the wine-press, dispeller of care, Healer of sorrow, mystic, frenzied, giver of wine, thousand-shaped, God of the night, shepherd-god, fawn-like, clothed in fawn-skin, Spear-thrower, common to all, giver of guests, yellow-haired, Prone to anger, stout of heart, lover of the mountain shade, wanderer on the mountains, Deep drinker, wanderer, wearer of many garlands, constant reveller, Mind-breaker, slender, wrinkled, clad in sheep-skin, Leaper, satyr, son of Semele, Jovial, bull-faced, slayer of Tyrrhenians, swift to wrath, Chaser of sleep, liquid, hymeneal, dweller in the woods, Mad for wild beasts, terrible, laughter-loving, wanderer, Golden-horned, graceful, relaxer of the mind, golden-filleted, Disturber of the soul, liar, bent on noise, tearer of the soul, Seasonable, eater of raw flesh, nurtured on the mountains, making clamour on the mountains. Let us chant the King who loves the call of EuhocEuhoe, the King Eiraphiotes.

div.head: 525.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
A similar Hymn to Apollo Let us hymn Paean the great god, Apollo; Immortal, gloriously formed, unshorn, soft-haired, Stern-hearted, king, delighting in arrows, giver of life, Joyous, laughing, slayer of giants, sweet-hearted,
Son of Zeus, slayer of the dragon, lover of the laurel, Sweet of speech, of ample might, far-shooter, giver of hope, Creator of animals, divine, Jove-minded, giver of zeal, Mild, sweet-spoken, sweet-hearted, gentle-handed, Slayer of beasts, blooming, charmer of the spirit, soft-speaking, Shooter of arrows, desirable, healer, charioteer, Weaver of the world, Clarian, strong-hearted, father of fruits, Son of Leto, pleasant, delighting in the lyre, resplendent, Lord of the mysteries, prophet, magnanimous, thousand-shaped, Lover of the bow-string, wise, stiller of grief, sober, Lover of community, common to all, taking thought for all, benefactor of all, Blessed, making blessed, Olympian, dweller on the hills, Gentle, all-seeing, sorrowless, giver of wealth, Saviour from trouble, rose-coloured, man-breaker, path-opener, Glittering, wise, father of light, saviour, Delighting in the dance, Titan, initiator, revered, Chanter of hymns, highest, stately, of the height, Phoebus, purifier, lover of garlands, cheerer of the spirit, Utterer of oracles, golden, golden-complexioned, golden-arrowed, Lover of the lyre, harper, hater of lies, giver of the soul, Swift-footed, swift-voiced, swift of vision, giver of seasons. Let us hymn Paean the great god, Apollo.

div.head: 526.—ALPHEIUS OF MYTILENE
div.p: SHUT, O god, the tireless gates of great Olympus; keep, O Zeus, the holy castle of heaven. Already sea and earth are subdued by the Roman arms, but the path to heaven is still untrodden.Imitated from No. 518, which cp.

div.head: 527.—ORACLE FROM HERODOTUSv. 26 : given in a dream to Hipparchus.
div.p: LION, with long-suffering heart, bear the unbearable. No evil man shall escape punishment.

div.head: 528.—PALLADAS
div.p: THE inhabitants of Olympus,Bronze statues of the heathen gods. having become Christians, live here undisturbed; for here they shall not be put on the fire in the melting-pot that produces necessary small change.

div.head: 529.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Bed of a Harlot made of Laurel
div.p: I who fled the bed of one,Daphne fled from Apollo to preserve her chastity. am made a bed for many.

div.head: 530.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: FORTUNE did not willingly give you advancement, but to show that her omnipotence reaches even as low as you.

div.head: 531.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THEY run equal to the winds; hence their name1 Isos, equal; aura, wind..

div.head: 532.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: TELL me, pumpkin, why even so late as this the watery tribe of cucumbers and pumpkins has not appeared. The Pumpkin's Reply ZEUS rained heavily and flooded the fields, which still hide our race against our will.

div.head: 533.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: On a Beast-fighter who escaped by means of a Pole A MAN fixed a pole on the ground, and throwing himself into the air made a somersault, and with his nimble feet passed over the back of the beast that was rushing at him. It failed to catch him; the people applauded loudly and the man escaped.

div.head: 534.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: On Artemis. ARTEMIS, sweating, forbodes war.

div.head: 535.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: DIONYSUS glories in ivy, Zeus in the aegis, the inhabitants of this city in their hospitality, and the city in her inhabitants.

div.head: 536.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: WATER in the sea travelled through water without getting wet.

div.head: 537.—NESTOR OF NICAEA
div.p: WHY did you make a disturbance and stop my song? A rider has learnt how to ride, and a singer how to sing. But if one who has learnt riding wants to sing, he is a failure in both riding and singingHe means that his detractors know nothing of poetry and should confine themselves to matters they understand..¹

div.head: 538, 539.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: These Nonsense Verses each contain all the Letters of the Alphabet.

div.head: 538, 539.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: These Nonsense Verses each contain all the Letters of the Alphabet.

div.head: 540.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Do not rapidly unfold to the end of the roll= Latin umbilicus. ² the book of Heraclitus the Ephesian. The path is very difficult, and all is mist and unilluminated darkness; but if one initiated introduce you, it is clearer than the bright sun.

div.head: 541.—ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA
div.p: THEOGENES sends to PisoSee No. 428. ³ the skilfully wrought bowls, and both of us together contain the heavens.

div.head: 542.—CRINAGORAS
div.p: NEVER fear, Philonides; write a piece composed for four parts or even more; for neither your singing nor the motions of Bathyllus' hands shall be lacking in grace.Bathyllus was a celebrated pantomime-dancer. Philonides, it would seem, sung his pieces himself. In these pieces one singer and one dancer took all the different parts, which, of course, were played one after the other.

div.head: 543.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: THE well-mounted troupe of bull-fighters from Thessaly, armed against the beasts with no weapons but their hands, spur their horses to run alongside the galloping bull, bent on throwing round its neck the noose of their arms. At the same time pulling it towards the ground by thus hanging themselves at the end of its neck and weighing down its head, they roll over even such a powerful brute.It is implied, of course, that the man throws himself off his horse. In Heliodorus (x. 30) the man is described as throwing his arms round the bull's neck and burying his face between its horns, and this seems to be what is meant here.

div.head: 544.—ADDAEUS
div.docAuthor: On a Figure of Galene cut by TryphonA famous gem-carver, some of whose work we possess.
div.p:
TRYPHON coaxed me, the Indian beryl, to be Galene, the goddess of Calm, and with his soft hands let
TRYPON coaxed me, the Indian beryl, to be Galene, the goddess of Calm, and with his soft hands let down my hair. Look at my lips smoothing the liquid sea, and my breasts with which I charm the windless waves. Did the envious stone but consent, you would soon see me swimming, as I am longing to do.

div.head: 545—CRINAGORAS
div.docAuthor: With a copy of Callimachus' HecaleHecale was an old woman who entertained Theseus at Marathon when he went to combat the Marathonian bull.
div.p: THIS chiselled poem is Callimachus', for in it he let out every reef of his Muse. He sings the hut of hospitable Hecale, and all the labours that Marathon imposed on Theseus. May the young strength of Theseus' hands be thine, MarcellusThe nephew of Augustus, whose early death Virgil bewails.,2 and a life of equal renown.

div.head: 546.—ANTIPHILUS
div.p: ONCE in a way let my couch be on the ship's poop, the weather-cloths above sounding with the blows of the spray, the fire breaking out from the stonesWithin which it is built.,3 and the pot upon them bubbling with empty noise. Let my eyes be on the unwashed cabin boy, and let my table be the first plank of the deck that offers; and a game of "Give and take" and the gossip of the sailors. The other day this happened to me, who love to be at hail fellow all round.

div.head: 548.—BIANOR
div.p: Ye children of the ox, how wrong of you to kill Hermonax, the straying baby boy¹ The poor child, in the innocence of his heart, went to you thinking you were bees, and you proved worse than vipers. Instead of giving him a dainty feast you drove your murderous stings into him, bitter bees, contrary in nature to your sweet gifts.

div.head: 549.—ANTIPHILUS
div.p: A. Ye streams of the fountain, why have ye fled? Where is all that water gone? What fiery sun has extinguished the ever-running spring? B. We are exhausted by tears for Agricola; his thirsty dust has absorbed all the drink we had to give.

div.head: 550.—ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA
div.p: I say not, Tenos, that thou art not famous, for of old the winged sons of BoreasZetes and Calais, slain in Tenos by Heracles. got thee renown. But Ortygia was celebrated too, and her name reached to the Rhipaean Hyperboreans. But now thou livest and she is dead. Who would have expected to see Delos more desert than Tenos?For the desert condition of Delos, see No. 408. Ortygia was an old name of the island. For the story of the annual first-fruits brought to Delos by the Hyperboreans see Herodotus iv. 33.

div.head: 551.—ANTIPHILUS
div.p:
Calchedon hates and punishes the ill-omened heron. Phoebus will tell for what reason it is always called the traitor-bird. When in the shallow sea standing on its thin shanks it was picking up its food
from the sand, then the foemen crossed to the city from opposite, learning at length to pass over the sea on foot. Stone the wicked bird, for it got from the enemy a heavy reward—conchs and seaweed, the traitorThe incident alluded to in this epigram is quite unknown, and the whole looks like a legend made up to account for the bad name this bird had at Chalcedon. Such popular explanations of local superstitions are legion. The last couplet is, of course, playful and ironical. 1 .

div.head: 552.—ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA
div.p: A sword made of Macedonian steel and taught valiance by the hand of Alexander, I come, Piso,cp. No. 428. longing for thy hand, and thus I greet thee: " I rejoice to find the right hand for which fate reserved me."

div.head: 553.—PHILIPPUS (?)
div.docAuthor: On the Foundation of Nicopolis by Augustus
div.p: To replace Leucas, and fertile Ambracia, and Thyrreum, and Anactorium, and Amphilochian Argos, and all the surrounding cities that the furious onslaught of war destroyed, Caesar founded me, Nicopolis, a divine city. Phoebus receives this reward for the victory of Actium.

div.head: 554.—MARCUS ARGENTARIUS
div.p: CLAM, Heraclea, pulchris juvenibus ore morigeraris. For long all the town says it of you. How do you venture to do such a shameful thing? Did anyone catch you by your beautiful hair and force you to it? Or is it because your pretty name is derived from Heracles that in your depravity you choose to kiss his wife Hebe (pubem juvenum).

div.head: 555.—CRINAGORAS
div.p: I AM an island, small, seven stadia long, though the geographers neglected (?) to measure me; but still you will see that when I am ploughed I give birth to fat crops, and that I am rich in every kind of fruit, and have plenty of fish to catch, and cool breezes in the dog-days, and the gentleness of unruffled harbours. I am near Phaeacian Corcyra. So that I might be made fun of, I took this name or which I am highly proud.I took this name of which I am highly proud.

div.head: 556.—ZONAS
div.p: NEREIDS, Nymphs of the shore, you saw Daphnis yesterday, when he washed off the dust that lay like down on his skin; when, burnt by the dog-star, he rushed into your waters, the apples of his cheeks faintly reddened. Tell me, was he beautiful? Or am I a goat, not only lame in my legs but in my heart too?

div.head: 557.—ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA
div.p: TARSUS, Cilician city, the runner Aries, son of Menec-cles, does not disgrace even Perseus, thy founder. Such are the boy's winged feet that not even Perseus would have shown him his back in the race. The youth is seen only at the start and the finish, never in the middle of the course.

div.head: 558.—ERYCIUS
div.p: CLESON'S billy-goat through the livelong night kept the she-goats awake with his snorting and jumping, for he had caught from afar the scent of a goat-slaying wolf that was approaching the fold built on the cliff. At length the dogs awakened from their bed, frightened away the huge beast, and sleep closed the eyes of the goats.

div.head: 559.—CRINAGORAS
div.p: I AM getting ready to sail to Italy, for I am on my way to my friends from whom I have been absent for so long. I am in search of a navigator to conduct me and bring me to the Cyclades and ancient Corcyra. But I beg for your help too, my friend Menippus, author of the learned circular tourA "periplus" of the Mediterranean in three books. and versed in all geography.

div.head: 560.—BY THE SAME
div.p: EARTHQUAKE, most dread of all shocks, whether thou art aroused by the upshaken currents of the sea or of the winds, spare my new-built house, for I know not yet any terror to equal the quivering of the earth.

div.head: 561.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: WHAT desert, sunless hill of Northern Scythia nourished thee, wild vine? Or was it the eternal ice of the snowy Celtic Alps or the iron-bearing soil of Spain—thee, who didst bear the sour grapes, the unripened clusters—that yielded this harsh juice?

div.head: 562.—CRINAGORAS
div.p: THE parrot that talks with human voice, taking leave of his wicker cage, flew to the woods on his many-coloured wings, and ever assiduous in greeting famous Caesar, did not forget that name even in the mountains. All the birds, sharpening their wits to learn, strove among each other which should be the first to say “ChaireHail”¹ to the god. Orpheus made the beasts obey him in the hills, and now every bird tunes its voice for thee, Caesar, unbidden.

div.head: 563.—LEONIDAS
div.p: If thou findest anywhere Democritus the lover of fruit, give him, Sir, this light message: that this is my season, the white-fruited fig-tree, and I bear for him the bread that wants no baking. Let him make haste, for my position is not secure, if he would pluck the fruit from my branches before they are stoned.

div.head: 564.—NICIAS
div.p: BEE, that revealest the presence of many-coloured spring in her delightful bloom; yellow bee, revelling in the prime of the flowers; fly to the sweetly-scented field and busy thyself with thy work, that thy waxen chambers may be filled.

div.head: 565.—CALLIMACHUS
div.p: THEAETETUS walked in an untroddenTheaetetus was seemingly a dramatic poet who worked on new lines and had not been successful. 1 road, and if this path does not lead, Bacchus, to thy ivy, the heralds shall call the names of others for a brief season, but Hellas shall proclaim his wisdom for ever.

div.head: 566.—BY THE SAME
div.p: A successful poet, Dionysus, is a man of few words. The most he says is “I conquer.” But he whom thy auspicious gale favours not, if he be asked “What luck?” says “Things go hard with me.” Let such phrases be his who broods on fancied injustice. But mine, O Lord, be the few syllables.

div.head: 567.—ANTIPATER OF SIDON (?)
div.p: ANTIODEMIS, the nursling of Aphrodite, who from her babyhood slept on purple cloth, the glance of whose melting eyes is softer than sleep, the halcyon of LysisLysis was the originator of a particular style of merry song, the singers of which were called Lysiodi., 2 the delightful toy of Methé, whose arms flow like water, who alone among women has no bones at all (for she was all cream-cheese), has crossed to Italy, that by her softening charm she may make Rome cease from war and lay down the sword.

div.head: 568.—DIOSCORIDES
div.p: NILE, rising in vast volume, thou hast carried away in thy random course the farm of Aristagoras and all his possessions. But the old man himself, abandoning all hope, swam, clinging to a clod of his own land, to his neighbour's half-destroyed farm, saying: "O long toil and useless work of my aged arms, ye are all become water, and this wave so sweet to farmers was the bitterest of floods for Aristagoras."

div.head: 569.—EMPEDOCLES
div.p: I have been a boy and a girl, a shrub, a bird, and a warm-blooded fish of the seaEmpedocles held the doctrine of metempsychosis..¹ Hail! my friends who dwell in the citadel of the great city, yellow Agrigentum, observers of righteousness. Know that I, no longer a mortal, but an immortal god, sojourn here honoured by all as is meet, crowned with fillets and flowery garlands.

div.head: 570.—PHILODEMUS
div.p: Xantho, modelled of wax, with scented skin, with a face like a Muse's, sweet-voiced, fair darling of the twin-winged Loves, play to me with thy scent-bedewed hands. "I must lie and sleep for long, dying not, on a single bed cut out of stone." Sing it to me again, Xantho dear; yea! yea! sing me that sweet song. [Dost thou not hear it, man who amassest interest of moneys? On a single bed cut out of stone thou shalt live for ever, unhappy wretch.]

div.head: 571.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Pindar screamedHe is compared to an eagle as elsewhere. loud from Thebes, the Muse of Simonides breathed delight with her sweet-strained voice, Stesichorus and Ibycus shine, Alcman was sweet, and Bacchylides' lips uttered dainty song, Persuasion attended on Anacreon, Lesbian Alcaeus sings varied strains on the Aeolian . . . But Sappho was not the ninth among men, but is tenth in the list of the lovely Muses.

div.head: 572.—LUCILIUS
div.p: "Let us begin our song from the Heliconian Muses"; so Hesiod wrote,Theog. l. 1. they say, while he kept his sheep. "Sing, O goddess, the wrath," and "Tell me, Muse, the man," said Calliope by the mouth of Homer. Now I have got to write a proem of some sort. But what shall I write now I am beginning to publish this second book? "Olympian Muses, daughters of Zeus, I should not have been saved unless Nero Caesar had given me money."

div.head: 573.—AMMIANUS
div.p: Sir notSIT not, O man, at another's table indulging thy belly with the bread of reproach, now weeping with the weeper and the sour-countenanced, and now laughing with the laughter, sharing both laughter and tears when thou hast no need of either.

div.head: 574.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I, too, thrice unhappy Anaxis, carted along the burden of this weary life that is no life. Yet I did not pull it for long, but spurning from me this distraught life I went to Hades.

div.head: 575.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: Heaven shall sooner quench its stars and the sun make bright the face of night; the sea shall sooner provide sweet water for mortals to draw, and the dead return to the land of the living, than oblivion of those ancient pages shall rob us of the glorious name of Homer.

div.head: 576.—NICARCHUS
div.docAuthor: On a Statue of Athena holding an Apple. Aphrodite speaks
div.p: Trito-born maiden, why dost thou vex me now by grasping in thy hand my prize of which thou hast robbed me. Thou rememberest how formerly, amid the rocks of Ida, Paris pronounced me fairest, not thee. Thine are the spear and shield, but mine is the apple. For the apple that old war was surely enough.

div.head: 577.—PTOLEMAEUS
div.p: I know that I am mortal, a creature of a day; but when I search into the multitudinous revolving spirals of the stars my feet no longer rest on the earth, but, standing by Zeus himself, I take my fill of ambrosia, the food of the gods.

div.head: 578.—LEON THE PHILOSOPHER
div.docAuthor: On the Conic Sections of Apollonius
div.p: DEEP, reader, and exceeding hard is the character of the things wherewith thisBy his insistence on the study of geometry. book is big, and it has every need of a Delian diverA proverb used of anything very difficult..¹ But if one dive into its depths and investigate accurately every recess, he shall gain the first prize in geometry, and be pronounced indisputably a learned man. Plato is witness and security for this.²

div.head: 579.—BY THE SAME
div.p: LOOK, Corinthian founder of Sicily, who once didst drink the famous waters of Syracusan Arethusa, upon the herald's staff as shaped by men of old timeWhat the connection is between the herald's staff and Syracuse no one has explained..³

div.head: 580.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE consul's month is first, the second cuts the furrow, the third rouses the Italians to war, the fourth announces the rosy-fingered season of spring. I, May, am the mother of roses. I, June, bring white lilies. This, July, is the binder of sheaves. August's wingsThe Etesian winds, which were supposed to cause the rising of the Nile. ⁴ make the Nile rise. This, September, is dear to Bacchus, rich in grapes. I, October, make honeyed wine, a delight for men. I, November, bring a joyful banquet to every manProbably olive oil..⁵ I, December, teach men to play on the lyre and to awaken sleepersAt the Saturnalia..⁶

div.head: 581.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Beast-fight in the Theatre
div.p: (The words are put in the mouth of the EmperorProbably inscribed on a picture of the Armenians' and Georgians' embassy to Constantine, accepting Christianity. 1) BOWMAN, lord of the Muses, far-shooter Phoebus, tell thy sister to arouse the mighty beasts just enough for them to touch men's bodies lightly and make the people cry out for pleasure in holy tones. Let me not, who sit on the throne of Jovecp. VI. 54. 2 the Merciful, look upon a man's death.

div.head: 582.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THESE Armenian tribes and the doughty Iberian people, full of zeal for Christ, came willingly under the yoke, submitting themselves to the law of our invincible emperors.Probably inscribed on a picture of the Armenians' and Georgians' embassy to Constantine, accepting Christianity.

div.head: 583.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: MY friend, if thou art learned, take me in thy hand; but if thou art ignorant of the Muses, cast away what thou canst not understand. I am not accessible to all, but the few admire Thucydides, son of Olorus, by birth an Athenian.

div.head: 584.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Statue at Delphi of Eunomus the Lyre-playercp. VI. 54. 4
div.p: THOU knowest, Apollo, how I, Eunomus the Locrian, conquered Spartis, but I tell it for those who ask me.

div.head: 585.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Dish with a Relief of Venus and Loves
div.p: HERE are four Loves. One fits the garland to his mother's brows, one has his lips at her bosom's fountain, two play at her feet, and the robe covers the place that is next to the thighs of Aphrodite, otherwise wholly undraped.

div.head: 586.—COMETAS CHARTULARIUS
div.p: A. TELL me, shepherd, whose are these rows of plants? B. The olive-trees belong to Pallas and the vines round them to Dionysus. A. And whose is the corn? B. Demeter's. A. To what gods do the flowers belong? B. To Hera and rosy Aphrodite. A. Dear Pan, stay here and ply the pipe with thy lips, for thou shalt find Echo on this sunny slope.

div.head: 587.—EUTOLMIUS ILLUSTRIUS
div.p:
On a Vessel for pouring Hot Water or Wine
I stand between Bacchus and the Nymphs, and ever pour into the cups that of which there is too little.It stood between the bowl of wine and the jar of water, and was used for filling the cups from both.

div.head: 588.—ALCAEUS
div.p: Even as thou seest, stranger, his stout heart in the bronze image, so Hellas saw the might of Clitomachus.See Pausanias vi. 15. For when he had put off the blood-stained cestus from his hands, he straightway fought in the fierce pancratium. In the third event he fouled not his shoulders in the dust, but wrestling without a fall won the three contests at Isthmus. Alone among the Greeks he gained this honour, and seven-gated Thebes and his father Hermocrates were crowned.

div.head: 589.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On a Statue of Hera suckling Heracles
A true stepmother did the sculptor render. Therefore he added no milk to the breast that was not kindred.

div.head: 590.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On a Group of Hephaestus, Athena, and Erechtheusi.e. Erichthonius. The epigram alludes to the very gross story of the circumstances of his birth. ³
“ Art united that which Nature did not,” said the sculptor. “ O mother without birth and bridegroom without marriage !”

div.head: 591.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Group of Ares and Aphrodite
div.p: THE painter in the interior of the house painted Ares and Aphrodite embracing each other. The bright Sun, coming in through the window, stood in astonishment as he gazed on them both. Till when shall the heavy wrath of the Sun endure? He would not banish his anger though it fell only on lifeless waxUsed in encaustic painting..¹

div.head: 592.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Shield representing the Birth of Christ
div.p: How simple was the artist to engrave the birth of the Prince of Peace on a shield!

div.head: 593.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE inspired hand infused into the marble both pity and fury, and made the stone Medea, under the empire of his art, remember all her griefs.

div.head: 594.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: PAINTER, who hast reproduced the form of Socrates, would thou couldst have put his soul into the wax!

div.head: 595.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: APELLES painted himself in the picture.

div.head: 596.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: SPARTA, glorious in war, gave birth to this Chilon, who was first in wisdom of the seven sages.

div.head: 597.—COMETAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: I was paralyzed from the hips to the soles of my feet, long deprived of my former activity, half-way between life and death, near to Hades, breathing only, otherwise an utter corpse. But skilled Philippus, whom you see in the picture, saved me, healing my chilling sickness; and now I, Antoninus, again tread on the earth and walk with my feet, and have feeling in every part.

div.head: 598.—THEOCRITUS
div.p: THIS man, Pisander of Camirus, first among the poets of old time, wrote of the son of Zeus, the lion-fighter, the nimble-handed, and told of all the labours he accomplished. Know that the city, after many months and years, set his very self up here in bronze.

div.head: 599.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Look well on this statue, stranger, and tell on thy return home: “ I saw in Teos the statue of Anacreon, a song-writer most excellent of those of old.” And adding that he took delight in young men, thou shalt exactly describe the whole man.

div.head: 600.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Doric is my tongue and Doric this man who invented comedy, Epicharmus. Bacchus, to thee as to a citizen, did they who dwell in Syracuse, mightiest of cities, dedicate him in bronze. Belike, mindful of his wise sayings, they paid him this guerdon. For many things useful for life he said to its children. Great thanks to him!i.e. Aphrodite will get her share.

div.head: 601.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This passing fair statue did Aeximenes erect to Aphrodite, the protectress of all navigation. Hail, sovereign Cypris! and if thou givest gain and welcome wealth thou shalt learn that a ship is most ready to go shares.i.e. Aphrodite will get her share.

div.head: 602.—EVENUS OF ATHENS
div.p: I who once supplicated Cyprus with my maiden hands, and, waving torches, prayed for marriage, after I had loosed my nuptial dress in the bridal chamber, suddenly saw spring from my thighs the marks of manhood. Now I am called a bridegroom instead of a bride, and crown the altars of Ares and Heracles instead of those of Aphrodite. Thebes once told of Tiresias, and now Chalcis greets in a chlamys her who formerly wore the snood.

div.head: 603.—ANTIPATER OF SIDON
div.p: These five votaries of Dionysus the Saviour are entering upon the rapid dance. One lifts on high the body of a grim lion, another an antlered Arcadian stag, a third a bird with lovely plumage, a fourth a kettle-drum, and the fifth a heavy brazen clapper. All are frenzied and distraught by the bacchic fury of the god.Possibly on the famous group of Thespian women by Praxiteles, which Mummius transferred to Rome.

div.head: 604.—NOSSIS
div.p: This is the picture of Thaumareta. Well did the painter render the bearing and the beauty of the gentle-eyed lady! Thy little house-dog would fawn upon thee if it saw thee here, thinking that it looked on the mistress of its home.

div.head: 605.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Callo had her portrait made exactly like herself, and hung the picture in the house of fair-haired

div.head: 606—640 are all Inscriptions on Baths 606.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Look at Cytherea whom Ares once loved, bathing here in the limpid stream. Look at her swimming, and fear not. It is not maiden Athena that you see, as Tiresias did.

div.head: 607.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: The Graces bathed here, and to reward the bath they gave to the water the brightness of their limbs.

div.head: 608.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Either such water gave birth to Cytherea, or Cytherea, by bathing in it, made the water such.

div.head: 609.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This bath is the playground of the Graces, for it only admits the Graces to sport within it.

div.head: 609A.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This is really the Graces' bath, for it cannot contain more than three.

div.head: 610.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This is a little work, but beautiful to look on, like a rose in a garden or a violet in a basket of flowers.
THERE is great charm in a little bath. Sweet love looks on those who bathe in the tiniest stream.
As a myrtle has little leaves, but sweet-scented, so this bath is small, but dear.

div.head: On the Bath of MariaThe Empress, wife of Honorius.
div.p: MomusThe god of fault-finding. wept when he saw the bath of Maria, exclaiming: “I have to leave you unvisited, as I leave Maria.”

div.head: On a small Bath next that called Zeuxippus
div.p: Be not wrath, Zeuxippus, with this bath that arises next thee. The little star called Erotylus shines sweetly though next the Great Bear.

div.head: On a Bath at Smyrna
div.p: THOU building, who of mortals made thee, who wast formerly dim, rich in light for bathers, and who, cleaning away the smoky grime that befouled thee, brightened thee thus? It was wise Theodorus who in this truly, as in everything, showed the cleanness of his heart. He being the treasurer and father

div.head: 616.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Here once when the Graces bathed, little Eros stole their immortal raiment and went off with it, leaving them naked and ashamed to appear outside the door.

div.head: 617.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On a too cold Bath
Who walled round a river, bathman? Who falsely styled this fountain a bath? “Aeolus, son of Hippotas, dear to the immortal gods,”¹ brought the winds here from their home. And why are these two planks placed here for the feet? Not for warmth, but for freezing. This is the place of Shivering and Frost-bite. Write thereon: “Bathe here in AugustMesori is the Egyptian name of August.,² for the north wind blows ever within.”

div.head: 618.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On a Bath in Byzantium
The old story of the lotus-eaters³ is no falsehood. This bath confirms its truth. For if a man once bathe in these pure waters he does not regret his country or desire his parents.

div.head: 619.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: Now I know, Cytherea, how thou didst conquer in the contest, stealing the vote of Alexander. It was here thou didst dip thy body, and so didst find means to overcome Hera who had bathed in the streams of Inachus.At Argos. It was the bath that won, and I fancy Pallas cried out thus: “I was conquered by the water, not by the Paphian.”

div.head: 620.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.docAuthor: On a Double Bath in which Men and Women Bathed
div.p: Near is the hope of love, but one cannot catch the women. A little door shuts out great Cyprus. But yet this is sweet; for in the matter of amorous desire hope is sweeter than reality.

div.head: 621.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Such women as have desire to please (and ye all have) come here, and ye shall win brighter charms. She who has a husband will give her husband pleasure, and the unmarried girl will stir many to offer her marriage. And she who makes her living by her body, if she bathe here, will have swarms of lovers at her door.

div.head: 622.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: If sweet desire for thy wedded wife possess thee, bathe here, and thou shalt appear to her brighter.

div.head: 623.—CYRUS
div.p: CYRUS with the Graces and her golden-arrowed boy bathed here and gave grace in payment.

div.head: 624.—LEONTIUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.docAuthor: On another Bath next the Public Baths in Byzantium
div.p: A CITIZEN built me at the gate of the public bath for excellence, not for competition. Let that serve many; I supply water and scent and charm to an intimate few.

div.head: 625.—MACEDONIUS THE CONSUL.
div.docAuthor: On another Bath in the Lycian Quarter (?)
div.p: LET my doorkeeper be the most faithful of men, keeping careful note of the time at which bathers enter me, lest anyone against his will see one of the Naiads naked in my waters, or Cyprus with the long-haired Graces: “For hard are the gods to him who sees them manifestly.”Hom. Il. xx. 131. Who would dispute Homer’s dictum?

div.head: 626.—MARIANUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: LOVE once bathed his mother Cyprus in this bath, himself warming its lovely water with his torch. Ah,

div.head: 627.—BY THE SAME
div.p: HERE under the plane-trees tired Love lay softly sleeping, having entrusted his torch to the Nymphs. Said the Nymphs among themselves: “Why not do it at once? Would that together with this we could put out the fire in men’s hearts.” But it was the torch that set fire to the water, and henceforth the Love-Nymphs pour forth here hot water for men to bathe in.

div.head: 628.—JOANNES GRAMMATICUS
div.docAuthor: On the Public Bath at Alexandria called the Horse
div.p: Our blessed sovereign aroused with a golden bit the fair-flowing Horse which long scourgings had laid low.The meaning is that the Emperor spent money on restoring the bath.

div.head: 629.—BY THE SAME
div.p: WOULD, Pindar, that I rather than others had washed thee in my stream. Then thou wouldst have called my water alone best.Referring to the beginning of Olymp. i. “Water is best.”

div.head: 630.—LEONTIUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: THESE are really the royal hot baths, for our fathers, admiring them, gave them this name. By no mortal fire is the bright water warmed, but the spring is born hot of its own accord. Nor dost thou require a cold stream for the bath, but tempered as thou dost desire it, it gushes forth.

div.head: 631.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.docAuthor: On the Hot Baths of Agamemnon near SmyrnaStill existing and so called. 1
div.p: I AM a place beloved by the Danai, coming to which they forgot the art of PodaliriusThe two sons of Asclepius, Podalirius and Machaon, were the surgeons of the Greek army before Troy..2 For after the battle they healed their wounds in my stream, expelling the poison of the barbarian spear. Hence I grew great and came to bear a roof, and as a token of fame received the name of Agamemnon.

div.head: 632.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: WHILE Earth in her inmost recesses has perpetual fire and boils with hidden flames, the hot vapour, ascending to the air owing to the pressure from below, belches forth streams of water heated by fire.

div.head: 633.—DAMOCHARIS GRAMMATICUS
div.p: THIS was the bath of Hera, Cyprus, and Pallas, when they were eager to get the golden apple. And perhaps now Paris will not be their judge, but their image reflected in the silver flood.

div.head: 634.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE Graces swore by the radiant lord of light rather to dwell here than with Cyprus.

div.head: 635.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THIS bath bears the name of the leafy laurel.

div.head: 636.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: IT was on seeing this bath that sagest Homer said : “ Allaying grief and anger, bringing oblivion of all evil.”Hom. Od. iv. 221.

div.head: 637.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: AFTER bathing her divine limbs here, Cypris straightway showed herself to Alexander, and carried off the prize of the apple.

div.head: 638.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE three Graces of Orchomenus made the bath, and therefore it has not room for four.

div.head: 639.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: CYPRIS, Love, the Graces, the Nymphs, Dionysus, and Apollo swore to each other to dwell here.

div.head: 640.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE immortals bathe when the bath is first opened, at the fifth hour the demi-gods, and later all the rubbish.

On a Bridge over the Sangarius
Thou too, Sangarius, after proud Italy and the peoples of the Medes, and all the barbarian host, art thus enslaved by the hand of our prince1 Justinian.,1 thy stream fettered by strong arches. Thou who wast formerly impassable to boats and indomitable, liest gripped in bonds of stone.

On a Latrine in the Suburbs of Smyrna
All the extravagance of mortals and their expensive dishes excreted here have lost their previous charm. The pheasants and fishes, and the mixtures pounded in the mortar, and all that variety of kickshaws, become here dung. The belly rids itself of all that the ravenous gullet took in, and at length a man sees that in the pride of his foolish heart he spent so much gold on nothing but dust.

On the Same
Why do you moan with the headache and groan bitterly for the heaviness you feel all over, and keep on smacking your belly, thinking to force out the work of your jaws? You would never have had all this trouble and labour if you had not largely exceeded yourself at table. When you are lying there

div.head: 644.—BY THE SAME
div.p: guzzling you have a high opinion of yourself, and delight your palate with the viands, deeming that happiness. But here you are in distress, and your belly only gets many smacks to pay for the sins of your gullet. BLEST are you, long-suffering labourer! You have only to put up, all your life, with the pains of hoeing and poverty. Simple are your meals, and you sleep in the woods, after satisfying your throat's vast thirst for water. Yet you are perfectly sound, and sitting here for a few moments lighten your belly. You don't rub down the lower part of your spine, or beat your thighs, but you get rid of the burden naturally. They are in evil case, the rich and those who associate with them, whom feasting pleases more than sound health.

div.head: 645.—MACEDONIUS THE CONSUL
div.p: I AM Sardis, the chief city of Lydia, who stand under flowery Tmolus, by the stream of Maeonian Hermus. I witnessed first the birth of Jove, for I refused to betray the secretly born son of my own Rhea. It was I, too, who nursed Bacchus, and I saw him shining with broader flame in the lightning-flash. First in my fields did Autumn, the giver of wine, milk from the udder of the grape-cluster the golden juice. Everything combined to adorn me, and old Time often saw me envied by the most flourishing cities.

div.head: 646.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: If you know of another city with the same name, Heraclea, know that I, the Pontic one, do not rank beneath it.

div.head: 647.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Rome, queen of the world, thy fame shall never perish, for Victory, being wingless, cannot fly from thee.

div.head: 648.—MACEDONIUS THE CONSUL
div.p: Native alike and foreigner are ever dear to me, for it is not the business of hospitality to enquire who, whence, and whose son.

div.head: 649.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Piety built up this house from its foundations to its lofty roof. For Macedonius did not build it out of wealth gained by despoiling with the sword the possessions of others, nor did he weep, a pauper, over an empty and profitless labour, deprived of the return justly due to his outlay. As rest from labour awaits the just, so may the works of pious men survive.

div.head: 650.—LEONTIUS
div.docAuthor: On an Inn situated between the ZeuxippusSee title of Book II. It was both a gymnasium and bath. 1 and the Hippodrome
div.p: On the one side I have close by me the Zeuxippus, a pleasant bath, and on the other the race-course After seeing the races at the latter and taking a bath in the former, come and rest at my hospitable table. Then in the afternoon you will be in plenty of time for the other races, reaching the course from your room quite near at hand.

div.head: 651.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.docAuthor: On a High House in Constantinople
div.p: From three sides I view the pleasant expanse of the sea, struck by the sunlight from all quarters. For when saffron-mantled Dawn envelops me, she is so pleased that she has no wish to go on to her setting.

div.head: 652.—JULIAN, PREFECT OF EGYPT
div.docAuthor: On a House situated on Level Ground
div.p: In summer I cool you and in winter I keep you warm, supplying from myself the deficiencies of the seasons.

div.head: 653.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.docAuthor: On a House situated on a Hill in Constantinople
div.p: “The gods set toil before virtue,”Hes. Works and Days, 289. 2 said the poet of Ascra, speaking prophetically of this house. For after mounting the long flight of steps with exhaustedLit. panting. feet, my hair was all soaked with sweat; but from the summit I looked on the fine view of the sea. Yea! perhaps a good room is a surer possession than virtue (?).

div.head: 654.—JULIAN, PREFECT OF EGYPT
div.p: SEEK other more profitable houses, ye robbers, for Poverty constantly keeps guard over this.

div.head: 655.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Banqueting Hall of Magnaura
div.p: THIS house was diligently completed by the emperors on whom the Cross bestowed a beneficent power, Heraclius and his son Constantine.Constantine III. shared the purple with his father Heraclius whom he succeeded 641 A.D.

div.head: 656.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the House called ChalcéLit. "The Bronze Gate." The name was transferred to the whole building which formed the vestibule of the palace. in the Palace built by Anastasius
div.p:
I AM the house of Anastasius, the emperor, slayer of tyrants,The Isaurian robber chiefs. and I alone far excel all cities of the Earth. I am a cause of wonder to all, since the architects, seeing my height, length, and vast breadth, were minded to leave the huge pile unroofed; but skilled Aetherius, the most eminent
I AM the house of Anastasius, the emperor, slayer of tyrants,⁴ and I alone far excel all cities of the Earth. I am a cause of wonder to all, since the architects, seeing my height, length, and vast breadth, were minded to leave the huge pile unroofed; but skilled Aetherius, the most eminent master of that laborious art, devised my shape, laying the first-fruits of his toil before our stainless emperor. Therefore, stretching on all sides my vast bulk, I surpass the celebrated wonders of the Italian land. Beauty of the Capitolian hall, give place to thy betters, even though thy roof of bronzethy golden roof dazzles the eye. Hide, Pergamus, thy splendid ornament, the grove of Rufinus,Quite unknown. The Rufinus referred to is probably the celebrated minister of Theodosius (circ. 400 A.D.). narrow now beside the halls of this limitless palace; and thou, Cyzicus, no longer sing of thy noble temple of Hadrian standing fast on the long cliff. The pyramids are not capable of vying with me, or the colossus, or the Pharos; I alone surpass a great legion of buildings. My prince himself, after his victory over the Isaurians, completed me, the house of the Dawn, shining with gold, on all sides exposed to the breezes of the four winds.

div.head: 657.—MARIANUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: WHERE the land is cut in two by the winding channel whose shores open the way to the sea, our divine emperorJustin II. (565-578 A.D.). erected this palace for his most illustrious consort Sophia. O, far-ruling Rome,i.e. Constantinople. thou lookest from Europe on a prospect in Asia the beauty of which is worthy of thee.

div.head: 658.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.docAuthor: On the Great Praetorium when newly decorated
div.p:
THE Emperor Justin,The same. clearing away its begrimed decorative work, brightened up the chief Law Court,
and thou, DomninusThe architect.,¹ by thy labours, expellest melancholy night from the halls of Themis and the life of mortals.

div.head: 659.—THEAETETUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: WHAT a blessing is a child in our old age! Domninus has made the courts of me, mother Justice, brighter. I shine through my child, and my child through me, each bestowing our glory on the other

div.head: 660.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Basilica of the Schools in Constantinople
div.p: I AM a place dedicated to Law. Here gushes forth an abundant fount of Roman Jurisprudence which runs perennially for all, and gives its whole stream to the youth here assembled.

div.head: 661.—JULIANUS, PREFECT OF EGYPT
div.docAuthor: On the Chair of the Sophist Craterus
div.p: I AM a tree peculiarly blessed; for, once, standing in the middle of the forest, I was nurtured by the shrill winds and was the tuneful seat of birds, but I was felled by the axe to gain still better fortune. For now I am watered by the powerful (crateros) speech, not of the birds, but of Craterus, and flourish, fed by this stream of eloquence.

div.head: 662.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: I AM a place formerly hideous, divided by brick walls, and here the bellies of strangers, natives, and countrymen thunderingly relieved themselves. But Agathias, the father of the city, transformed me and made me distinguished instead of most ignoble.

div.head: 663.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.docAuthor: On a Garden by the Sea
div.p: THE sea washes terra firma, and the expanse of the dry land is navigable and blooms with marine foliage. How skilled was he who mingled the deep with the land, sea-weed with garden plants, the floods of the Nereids with the founts of the Naiads !

div.head: 664.—BY THE SAME
div.p: HERE the Naiads, Nereids, and Hamadryads dispute as to who has the best title to the property. The Grace in their midst sits as judge, but cannot give judgment, as its charm is common to all.

div.head: 665.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: GIVE way to me, thou holy hill of DaphneThe celebrated park near Antioch in Syria. See Gibbon, chap. xxiii.,1 lying far from the sea, thy beauty but that of rustic solitude.

div.head: 666.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Eros is not big, but he is pretty. So I am not great among gardens, but am full of charm.

div.head: 667.—ARABIUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: I am rich in waters, gardens, groves, vineyards, and the generous gifts of the neighbouring sea. Both the fisherman and the husbandman offer me pleasing presents from sea and land, and those who rest in me are soothed either by the song of birds or the sweet call of the ferryman.

div.head: 668.—MARIANUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.docAuthor: On a Suburban Park in Amasia called Eros
div.p:
Verily it is lovely, the grove of Eros, where these beautiful trees are stirred by the gentle breath of Zephyr, where the dewy meadow is bright with flowers, sending up a wealthy show of purple-fringed cups, while the roses of three fountains in a line one after the other spout forth the streams of the sweet Naiad. Here Iris, the ancient river, swims past the woods, resort of the soft-haired Hamadryads,
Verily it is lovely, the grove of Eros, where these beautiful trees are stirred by the gentle breath of Zephyr, where the dewy meadow is bright with flowers, sending up a wealthy show of purple-fringed cups, while the roses of three fountains in a line one after the other spout forth the streams of the sweet Naiad. Here Iris, the ancient river, swims past the woods, resort of the soft-haired Hamadryads, and in the fruitful vineyard the fat berries of the olive-trees flourish everywhere above the great clusters of raisins set out to dry. Around sing the nightingales, and the cicada hymns an answering harmony. Do not, stranger, pass by my open gate, but enter the house and partake of my simple hospitality.

div.head: 669.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Come here for a little, traveller, and reclining in the greenwood shade rest thy limbs from thy long and toilsome journey. Here amongst the plane-trees the fresh streams of water running at its will leap forth beautifully from many-mouthed fountains. Here in spring the soft violets mixed with roses empurple the ground. Look how, engarlanding the fresh meadow, the luxuriant ivy twines its flowing hair. The river runs between its foliaged banks, grazing the base of the self-sown grove. Such is Eros. What other name would be appropriate for a place replete in every way with charm and loveliness?

div.head: 670.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Mole in Smyrna on which there was a Cistern
div.p: A. Who made the deep dry land, who amid the surges built out of marble a shore washed on both sides by the sea? And who enabled the sailors to obtain water in the midst of the waves, drawing it with their hands even from the deck? B. This resourceful man, noble Venetius, who surpassed Theseus and PelopsIt is difficult to see why these names are selected. They were both, of course, founders of cities. by his creations.

div.head: 671.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Lighthouse in the same City
div.p: A. Who executed so great a work? What is his city and what his office? B. Ambrosius of Mylasa, the proconsul, built the lighthouse.

div.head: 672.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Though thou journeyest over the sea-bound circle of the whole dry land, thou shalt nowhere see a place superior to this which renowned Ioannes, glorifying her the queen of all this land, has made so admirable; for from the sea itselfThe meaning is quite obscure. he won unceasing delight for Homer's city.

div.head: 673.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Place in the same City
div.p: Asclepius did this work, too, for Hippolyta.i.e. a patrician of Constantinople.

div.head: 674.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I am the tower that helps straying mariners, lighting up the blaze of Poseidon's comforting torch. Ammonius, who is the father of our emperor,The meaning is quite obscure. re-erected me by his labour when, borne down by the loud-roaring gales, I was about to fall. To him the sailors, escaped from the wild waves, lift up their hands as to the glorious Earth-shaker.

div.head: 675.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: SAIL to me fearlessly, ye mariners, no longer dreading the rayless gloom of the night. For all wanderers burns my far-flashing torch, keeping alive the memory of my builders the AsclepiadaeThe medical guild at Smyrna..¹

div.head: 676.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Fountain in the Asiatic Mount Olympus
div.p: I yield to the Nymphs of Prusa, and salute, too, those of the PythianIn Bithynia. waters as my superiors. But let the whole company of Naiads after Pythia and after Prusa give way to my Nymphs.

div.head: 677.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
