div.p: Musonius built me with great labour, this large and imposing house, exposed to the north wind's blasts. Yet did he not avoid the dark house of Fate, but abandoning me he dwells underground. In a narrow bed of earth he lies, and I, his chiefest delight, am given up to strangers.

div.head: 678.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: WHAT a great and laborious work is this, too, that thou hast achieved, Agaclides, gaining great glory by thy daring! Thou hast enriched this parched land of the ancient Nymph Bassa with water and baths.

div.head: 679.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: ALL cities worship Axiochus, for, on his progress, like a god he has healed the ills of each. Especially on rugged Assus did he bestow running water, cutting through the hard face of many rocks. No longer run off to a distance, all ye travellers. I overflow with the cold water of Axiochus.

div.head: 680.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Sea-side Garden at Antioch in which was a Bath
div.p: THOU seest in me the three Graces, stranger. Poseidon wrought the one from the neighbouring sea, the second is the work of my garden rich in produce, and the remaining one is supplied by this bath.

div.head: 681.—LEONTIUS SCHOLASTICUS
div.docAuthor: On a Shell with a Carving of Aphrodite
div.p: It is a great favour I grant thee, Dionysus. Cypris bathes in me, and from her I bring thee the cup.

div.head: 682.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Obelisk in the HippodromeThe prefect of the city. 1
div.p: It was only the Emperor Theodosius who undertook to raise the four-sided column which had ever lain a burden on the earth. He committed the task to Proclus,The prefect of the city. and so great a column stood erect in thirty-two days.

div.head: 683.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: ALPHEUS is a male water, Arethusa a female, and Love accomplished their marriage by mixing the waters.

div.head: 684.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Fountain on the Island TaphosOne of the Echinades islands at the mouth of the Adriatic.
div.p: I AM the fountain Nychea, daughter of Ocean and Tethys, for so the Teleboae named me. I pour forth a bath for the Nymphs and health for mortals. It was Pterelas, the son of Ares, who placed me here.

div.head: 685.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On Camarina the Sicilian LakeThe first line alone is elsewhere cited as the response of Apollo when the people of Camarina asked him if they should drain the marsh near their city.
div.p: MOVE not Camarina, for it is best unmoved, lest, if thou move it, thou make the lesser greater.

div.head: 686.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Eastern Gate of Thessalonica
div.p: EXULT in thy heart, stranger, when thou seest above the gate the prefect BasilAs the terms of the epigram suit the emperor Basil I., who conquered the Arabs in Mesopotamia and was celebrated as a legislator, it probably refers to him in spite of the title "Prefect" given him.,³ destroyer of the valour of insolent Babylon and light of incorrupt justice. Thou goest to the place of good government, the mother of excellent sons. Thou hast no need to fear the barbarian or sodomites.i.e. the Arabs. The Greeks at the time charged the Oriental nations with this vice. There is no reference to measures for its suppression. The Spartan for a wall has his arms, and thou a royal statue (or the statue of Basil.)

div.head: 687.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I who painted the form would fain have painted also the character, but the limits of art checked my eagerness. Call me eloquent Alexander, my friend.In this line it seems to be the portrait which speaks.

div.head: 688.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This gate, built of polished stone, both an ornament for Argos and an object of admiration for travellers, was erected by Cleadas, the husband of gentle and noble Clea. He was the excellent hierophant of the sanctuary of Lerna, and enjoyed the generosity of powerful monarchs.A stone from Argos, now at Oxford, has the dedication, also in verse, by this Cleadas of his father's statue.

div.head: 689.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Gate of Eugenius in Constantinople
div.p: This JulianNo doubt the Emperor. ³ who built the walls that protect the city erected the trophy in memory of his vigilance. He studied rather to slay his enemies at a distance than to stir up war before the city.

div.head: 690.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Gate called Xylocercus at Constantinople
div.p: TheodosiusThe Younger (A.D. 408-450). ⁴ the emperor and Constantine, prefect of the East, built this wall in sixty days.

div.head: 691.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Gate of Rhesius at Constantinople
div.p: In sixty days Constantine the prefect built this strengthening wall for his sceptred sovereign.

div.head: 692.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This is the work of Vivianus, of whom East and West sing with honour because of his just government.

div.head: 693.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Demetrius the governor erected this temple of Fortune, feeling compassion for the city, like the son of Hierius he was. He built it on his own initiative, not the city's, and at his own, not at the public expense.

div.head: 694.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: The son of Messalinus built this magnificent arch.

div.head: 695.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: You see what great beauty lies in the disorderly order of the veins in the stone.

div.head: 696.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Portico of the Basilica in Constantinople
div.p: TheodorusIn the reign of Theodosius II., having built for the city four porticos, deserves to govern the city a fourth time.

div.head: 697.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On another part of the same Portico
div.p: It beseemed thee, Theodorus, to adorn the columned temple of FortuneThe same as the Basilica. 1 by such a wonderful work, and to give splendid gifts to Constantinople, city of the golden shield, which made thee consulA.D. 399. 2 and sees thee for the third time prefect.

div.head: 698.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: You look on this famous city of MopsusA mythical seer who had an oracle here and elsewhere in Cilicia.,3 which the seer once built, hanging its beauty over the river.

div.head: 699.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: From this fountain Alexander of Macedon drank splendid water, and said its streams were like his mother's milk. Hence he named it Olympias, as this stone testifies.

div.head: 700.—SIMONIDES
div.p: Polygnotus of Thasos, the son of Aglaophon, painted the sack of the citadel of Troy.On the Lesche of the Cnidians at Delphi.

div.head: 701.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens
div.p: This house is worthy of Zeus. Not even Olympus would blame Zeus for descending here from heaven.

div.head: 702.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE Athenians set up this house to Zeus, so that, descending from Olympus to earth, he might find another Olympus.

THE sources of the river Tearus supply the best and most beautiful water of any river, and to these came, leading his army against Sardis, the most beautiful and best of all men, Darius, son of Hystaspes, king of Persia and all the continent.

div.head: 704.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a RotundaAt Aphrodisias in Caria. The stone has been found.
div.p: LONG time wears out even stone, but immortal is the renown of the good deeds of Asclepiodotus in giving so many and such splendid gifts to his native place. Now in addition to them all should be reckoned this hollow structure with its dome.

div.head: 705.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THIS gift, received from the city of TermessusIn Lycia. in recognition of his upright jurisdiction, Eusebius dedicates to the god whose servant he is.

div.head: 706.—ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA (?)
div.p:
I AM a holy tree. Beware of injuring me as thou passest by, stranger, for I suffer pain if I am muti-
lated. Remember that my bark is still virginal, not like that of savage wild pear-trees. Who does not know what the race of poplars is like? If thou dost bark me, as I stand here by the road, thou shalt weep for it. Though I am but wood, the Sun cares for me.The daughters of the Sun continued to weep for their brother Phaethon until turned into poplars.

div.head: 707.—TULLIUS GEMINUS
div.p: I AM reckoned among rivers, but rival the sea in volume, Strymon, the fresh-water sea of Thrace. I am both a deep stream and a field yielding crops through my water, for water-chestnuts sweeter than the fruits of Demeter rise from me.The inhabitants made a kind of sweet bread from the seeds of this plant (trapa natans); it is still used in some places for the purpose, and has, in fact, been introduced as a food-plant into American rivers. The depths, too, are productive in Thrace, and we deem, Nile, that the bearer of the crop is superior to its feeder.

div.head: 708.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: THE barbarian bridged the Hellespont in his daring folly, but Time dissolved all that labour. Now Dicaearchia has made the sea a continent, and given the depths the form of dry land. She fixed firmly in the depths a vast supporting structure of stone, and with the hands of the Giants made the water beneath stand still. We could always sail over the sea, but insecure as it was for sailors who travelled on it, it has now promised to remain secure for foot-travellers.cp. Book VII. 379, of which this is an imitation.

div.head: 709.—BY THE SAME
div.docAuthor: On the Bronze Statue of the Eurotas by Eutychides
div.p: THE artist moulded Eurotas fresh from his bath of fire, as if still wet and immersed in his stream. For

div.head: 710.—Anonymous
div.p: Legend invented the false story of Ossa and Pelion mounted on Olympus. But even yet the Egyptian pyramids reach the golden Pleiads with their summits.

div.head: 711.—ZENOBIUS THE GRAMMARIAN
div.p: The painter wished to depict Grammar herself, and having painted Victor, said: “I have attained my end.”

div.head: 712.—METRODORUS
div.p: When Law in her old age had been visited by Joannes, she said, rejuvenated: “Solon, I have you again with me.”

div.head: 713.—Anonymous
div.p: I am Myron’s little heifer, set up on a base. Goad me, herdsman, and drive me off to the herd.

div.head: 714.—Anonymous
div.p: Why, Myron, didst thou set me here by the altars? Wilt thou not lead me into the house?

div.head: 715.—ANACREON (?)
div.p: HERDSMAN, pasture thy herd far from here, lest taking Myron's heifer to be alive thou drive it off with the rest.

div.head: 716.—BY THE SAME
div.p: MYRON pretended this heifer to be the work of his hands, but it was never formed in the mould, but turned into bronze owing to old age.

div.head: 717.—EVENUS
div.p: EITHER a complete hide of bronze clothes here a real cow, or the bronze has a soul inside it.

div.head: 718.—BY THE SAME
div.p: PERHAPS Myron himself will say this: “I did not mould this heifer, but its image.

div.head: 719.—LEONIDAS
div.p: MYRON did not mould me; he lied; but driving me from the herd where I was feeding, he fixed me to a stone base.

div.head: 720.—ANTIPATER OF SIDON
div.p: IF Myron had not fixed my feet to this stone I would have gone to pasture with the other cows.

div.head: 721.—BY THE SAME
div.p: CALF, why dost thou approach my flanks, and why dost thou low? The artist put no milk in my udder.

div.head: 722.—ANTIPATER
div.p: Pass by the heifer, cowherd, and whistle not to her from afar. She is expecting her calf to suckle it.

div.head: 723.—BY THE SAME
div.p: The lead and stone hold me fast, but, otherwise, thanks to thee, sculptor Myron, I would be nibbling lotus and rushes.

div.head: 724.—BY THE SAME
div.p: I think the heifer will low. Of a truth it is not Prometheus alone who moulds living creatures, but thou too, Myron.

div.head: 725.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Myron was looking for his own cow among the others, and found it with difficulty by driving the rest away.

div.head: 726.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: The cow, its mother, moulded this heifer giving birth to it, but the hand of Myron did not mould it, but gave birth to it.

div.head: 727.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: The horned cow would have spoken, though made of bronze, if Myron had worked entrails inside it.

div.head: 728.—ANTIPATER
div.p: THE heifer, I think, will low, and if it delays it is the fault of the senseless bronze, not Myron's.

div.head: 729.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: LET someone attach me to the solid plough and put a yoke on my neck, for as far as depends on thy art, Myron, I will plough.

div.head: 730.—DEMETRIUS OF BITHYNIA
div.p: IF a calf sees me, it will low; a bull will mount me, and the herdsman drive me to the herd.

div.head: 731.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: MYRON placed me, the heifer, here, but the herdsmen throw stones at me thinking I have strayed.

div.head: 732.—MARCUS ARGENTARIUS
div.p: STRANGER, if thou seest my herdsman, give him this message, that the sculptor Myron tied me up here.

div.head: 733.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: STRANGER, it was Myron who moulded this cow, on which this calf fawns as if it were alive, taking it for its mother.

div.head: 734.—DIOSCORIDES
div.p: IN vain, bull, thou rushest up to this heifer, for it is lifeless. The sculptor of cows, Myron, deceived thee.

div.head: 735.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: A CALF died beside thy heifer, Myron, deceived into thinking that the bronze had milk inside.

div.head: 736.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: ALACK! Myron, thou didst not have time to complete thy casting, but the bronze hardened before thou couldst put life into it.

div.head: 737.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THOU strikest the bronze heifer. Art deceived thee much, herdsman: Myron did not add life.

div.head: 738.—JULIAN, PREFECT OF EGYPT
div.p: NATURE and Queen Art strove in the matter of this cow, and Myron gave to each a prize of equal value. When one looks at it Art robs nature of her superiority, but when one touches it Nature is nature.

div.head: 739.—BY THE SAME
div.p: MYRON deceived thee too, gadfly, that thou plungest thy sting into the hard flanks of the bronze cow. But the gadfly is excusable. What wonder! when Myron deceived even the eyes of the herdsmen.

div.head: 740.—GEMINUS
div.p: It is the base to which it is attached that keeps back the heifer, and if freed from this it will run off to the herd. For the bronze lows. See how much alive the artist made it. If you yoke a fellow to it, perhaps it will plough. to the herd. For the bronze lows. See how much alive the artist made it. If you yoke a fellow to it, perhaps it will plough.

div.head: 741.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THOU wast bronze, deceptive heifer, and the husbandman came up to thee dragging a plough and carrying a yoke. He far excels all other artists, Myron, who by his labour made thee alive, just like a labouring cow.

div.head: 742.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: TAKE off from my neck, husbandman, the collar, and free me from the iron furrow-cutter; for Myron did not make my bronze into flesh, but his art gave me the aspect of being alive, so that often I even wished to low. He did not, however, let me go to work, but tied me to a base.

div.head: 743.—THEODORIDAS
div.p: THESE cows are Thessalian, and by the gates of Itonian AthenaHer temple was between Pherae and Larissa in Thessaly. cp. Book VI. 130. 1 they stand, a beautiful gift, all of bronze, twelve in number, the work of Phradmon, all wrought from the spoil of the naked Illyrians.

div.head: 744.—LEONIDAS
div.p: THE goatherds Soson and Simalus, rich in goats, stranger, seeing that they come from . . . dense with lentises, dedicated here to Hermes, the giver of cheeses and milk, this brazen, bearded goat, the lord of the flock.

div.head: 745.—ANYTE
div.p: Look on the horned goat of Bacchus, how haughtily with saucy eye he looks down on his flowing beard, exulting that often in the mountains the Naiad, caressing his cheeks, took those locks in her rosy hand.

div.head: 746.—KING POLEMO
div.p: This little jasper stone has a seal of seven cows looking like oneIf not corrupt, it must mean that they were represented one standing behind the other, only the heads of six showing.,¹ and all looking at us as if alive. Perhaps the cows would have run away, but now the little herd is confined in the golden pen.

div.head: 747.—PLATO
div.p: The little jasper stone is carved with five cows all looking alive as they feed. Perhaps they would run away, but now the little herd is confined in the golden pen.

div.head: 748.—PLATO THE YOUNGER
div.docAuthor: On Dionysus carved on an Amethyst
div.p: The stone is amethysti.e. "against drunkenness.",² but I am the toper Dionysus. Either let it teach me to be sober, or learn itself to get drunk.

div.head: 749.—OENOMAUS
div.docAuthor: On Love carved on a Bowl
div.p: Why Love on the bowl? It is enough for the heart to be set on fire by wine. Add not fire to fire.

div.head: 750.—ARCHIAS
div.docAuthor: On Cows carved on a Ring
div.p: Looking at the cows and the jasper on my hand, you will fancy that the cows breathe and the jasper puts forth grass.

div.head: 751.—PLATO THE YOUNGER
div.p: The stone is HyacinthusJacinth.,¹ and on it are Apollo and Daphne. Of which was Apollo rather the lover?

div.head: 752.—ASCLEPIADES or ANTIPATER OF THESSALONICA
div.p: I am Drunkenness, the work of a skilled hand, but I am carved on the sober stone amethyst. The stone is foreign to the work. But I am the sacred possession of Cleopatra: on the queen's hand even the drunken goddess should be sober.

div.head: 753.—CLAUDIANUS
div.p: The snow-white crystal, fashioned by the hand of man, showed the variegated image of the perfect universe, the heavenBecause it was spherical.,² clasping within it the deep-voiced sea.

div.head: 754.—BY THE SAME
div.p: A. Tell me, ice, water frozen into stone, who froze thee. B. Boreas. A. And who melted thee? B. The South wind.

div.head: 755.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On Scylla in BronzeProbably in the Hippodrome at Constantinople.
div.p: Unless the bronze glistened and betrayed the work to be a product of Hephaestus' cunning art, one looking from afar would think that Scylla herself stood here, transferred from sea to land, so threatening is her gesture, such wrath does she exhibit, as if dashing ships to pieces in the sea!

div.head: 756.—AEMILIANUS
div.p: As far as it depends on thy art, Praxiteles, the stone could wax wanton. Let me loose and I will join in the revel again. It is not that my old age is feeble, but the fettering stone grudges the Sileni their sport.

div.head: 757.—SIMONIDES
div.p: Iphion of Corinth painted this. There is no fault in his hand, since the achievement far excels the expectation.

div.head: 758.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Cimon painted the door on the right, and Dionysius that on the right as you go out.

div.head: 759.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Of one stone are chariot, charioteer, horses, yoke, reins, whip.

div.head: 760.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: Of one stone are chariot, charioteer, horses, yoke, reins, and Victory.

div.head: 761.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On a Painting of a Bunch of Grapes
I was almost grasping the cluster in my fingers, more than deceived by the sight of the colours.

div.head: 762.—ABLABIUS ILLUSTRIUS
div.p:
On the Quoit of Asclepiades
Hephaestus wrought me with long labour, but Cytherea took me secretly from her husband's chamber and gave me to Anchises as a souvenir of their stolen intercourse. Asclepiades found me among the descendants of Aeneasi.e. the Romans. Who Asclepiades was we do not know. It looks as if he were an exceptionally lucky collector of antiquities..¹

div.head: 763.—JULIANUS, PREFECT OF EGYPT
div.p:
On a Magistrate's Axe
If thou art guilty of crime, thy eyes see here an axe, but if thou art innocent, I am only silver to thee.

div.head: 764.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.p: No powerful beast, or fish of the sea, or bird do I catch in my meshes, but men willing to be caught. My defensive art, in no wise inferior to a city's wall, keeps a man who would avoid the sting of flies uneaten as he takes his siesta after the midday meal. I bring him the gift of undisturbed slumber, and save the slaves themselves from their service of chasing the flies away.

div.head: 765.—BY THE SAME
div.p: I am hung round wealthy bridal beds and am the net, not of the huntress Artemis, but of the tender Queen of Paphos. I cover the sleeper with a many-meshed web, so that he in no way loses the life-giving breeze.

div.head: 766.—AGATHIAS SCHOLASTICUS
div.p: It is the office of nets to surround the winged tribes and enclose their quick brood; but I take pleasure in chasing them away and do not cover them round, but rather keep them off when they attack. Not a single mosquito, however small, will manage to get through the fabric of my net. One may say that I save from death the winged creatures while I guard the beds of men. Can anyone be more righteous than I am?

div.head: 767.—BY THE SAME
div.p: SEATED by this table made of pretty stones, you will start the pleasant game of dice-rattling. Neither be elated when you win, nor put out when you are beaten, blaming the little die. For even in small things the character of a man is revealed, and the dice proclaim the depth of his good sense.

div.head: 768.—BY THE SAME
div.p: THESE things are all play. The shifting current of Fortune is pictured in these unreasoning dice, and, now a winner, now a loser, you will perceive in them the unstable image of mortal life. We praise him who in life and in play imposes a limit on his joy and grief.

div.head: 769.—BY THE SAME
div.p: To men of gentle disposition this is play, but to those lacking in self-restraint it is madness and wandering of the wits and self-imposed pain. If you come in last, speak no word of offence to God, nor boil over and snort loudly. One should neither give oneself trouble in a matter of play, nor play in serious matters. Learn to allot to the hour what befits it.

div.head: 770.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.docAuthor: On a Cup belonging to his own Unmarried Daughter
div.p: ANICETIA moistens her golden lips in me, and may I give her the bridal draught too.

div.head: 771.—JULIAN, PREFECT OF EGYPT
div.docAuthor: On a Cup on which Swimming Fish were chased or painted
div.p: THETISi.e. the sea. really received Bacchus: at length the truth of Homer's storyHom. Il. vi. 136. is confirmed.

div.head: 772.—PHOCAS THE DEACON
div.docAuthor: On a Cup in which the Leavings are collected
div.p: I AM dear to the cup-bearer alone, because I collect for him the wine that is left.

div.head: 773.—PALLADAS
div.p: THE smith transformed Love into a frying-pan, and not unreasonably, as it also burns.

div.head: 774.—GLAUCUS OF ATHENS
div.p: THE Bacchante is of Parian marble, but the sculptor gave life to the stone, and she springs up as if in Bacchic fury. Scopas, thy god-creating art has produced a great marvel, a Thyad, the frenzied slayer of goats.

div.head: 775.—BY THE SAME
div.p: THE Bacchante has made the son of Cronos a Satyr, and he rushes to the frenzied dance as if he were in Bacchic furyZeus disguised himself as a Satyr in order to possess Antiope at the Bacchic revels..¹

div.head: 776.—DIODORUS
div.p: THE colour and the beauty is worthy of Zeuxis; but Satyreius painted me on a little crystal and gave the pretty miniature to Arsinoe. I am the queen's own image, and no whit inferior to a large picture.

div.head: 777.—PHILIPPUS
div.p: Look how proudly the art of the worker in bronze makes this horse stand. Fierce is his glance as he arches his neck and shakes out his wind-tossed mane for the course. I believe that if a charioteer were to fit the bit to his jaws and prick him with the spur, thy work, Lysippus, would surprise us by running away; for Art makes it breathe.

div.head: 778.—BY THE SAME
div.p: On a Tapestry In me Carpo, imitating all by her shuttle's labour at the loom, depicted accurately all the fruitful land, encompassed by Ocean, that obeys great Caesar, and the blue sea as well. I come to Caesar as a present . . . , for it was the queen's duty to offer the gift long due to the gods.i.e. to the emperors. The corrupt word in l. 5 (or possibly καρπῷ in l. 3, where καρπῷ is a conjecture) conceals the clue to the identity of the queen. She was probably Oriental.

div.head: 779.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On the Base of the Sun-dial in the Arch of the Basilica
Look, Light of Freedomi.e. "the Sun," but the phrase is obscure. I suppose it means "Sun, who now shinest on a free state," and refers to the same matter as the epithet "tyrannicide.",¹ on this gift of our emperor JustinJustin II. The title "tyrannicide" refers to the suppression of some real or fancied usurper.,² the tyrannicide, and his wife Sophia, this skilled bronze indicator of the hours from one to twelve. It had been stolen, and Julianus the Praetorian Prefect recovered it with incorruptible hands.

div.head: 780.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On a Sun-dial
This is the learned stone which contains all the heavens, and which a little regulator adapts to every position of the sunIt was so regulated that it was adapted to every day in the year, each day—from sunrise to sunset—containing twelve hours. What was the mechanism?.³
div.note: It was so regulated that it was adapted to every day in the year, each day—from sunrise to sunset—containing twelve hours. What was the mechanism?

div.head: 781.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On the Lattice of a House
If you shut me I am open, and if you open me you will shut me. Being such, I cannot guard your houseA very silly epigram. The lattice, having holes in it, is open when shut and shut when open, as the light no longer comes through it..⁴
div.note: A very silly epigram. The lattice, having holes in it, is open when shut and shut when open, as the light no longer comes through it.

div.head: 782.—PAULUS SILENTIARIUS
div.p: HERE men divide the course of bright Phaethon into twelve hours and measure the sun's path by water, lifting up their minds from earth to heaven.

div.head: 783.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Hermaphrodite which stood in a Bath
div.p: To men I am Hermes, but to women appear to be Aphrodite, and I bear the tokens of both my parents. Therefore not inappropriately they put me, the Hermaphrodite, the child of doubtful sex, in a bath for both sexes.

div.head: 784.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: REVILE not small things. Small things possess charm. Cypris' son, Eros, was small too.

div.head: 785.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Vaulted Chamber on the West Side of the Forum
div.p: MENAS built the golden structure for all travellers, glorifying the city of our kings rich in gold.

div.head: 786.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THE inhabitants erected to the god this beautiful altar, placing it here as a sign to mark the boundary of Leuce and Pteleus. The arbiter of the divi-sion is the king of the immortals himself, Cronus' son.1 From Demosth. vii. 39. The places are in the Thracian Chersonese.

div.head: 787.—SOPHRONIUS THE PATRIARCH
div.p: STRANGER, who formerly on your arrival by land or by sea wandered about with homeless feet, approach now and stay your steps here, where, if you wish to dwell, you will find a lodging all ready. But if you, citizen, demand who made me, it was Eulogius, the good bishop of Alexandria.

div.head: 788.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: UNDER thy rule, noble Fortune, the blest life of men enjoys the light of prosperity. For at thy nod all things bring glory to him whom thou permittest to caress thy divine neck with his right hand. To thy will illustrious kings bow, and the blest leaders of the learned company. Ships, too, rest safer in harbour, saved at sea by thy help, and cities enjoy tranquility, and peoples, and the ambrosial meads of the verdant plain. Therefore looking on thy servant .

div.head: 789.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: LOOK on me, the adorner of learned discourse, who direct my art by the rule of eloquence.

div.head: 790.—ANTIPATER
div.docAuthor: On the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
div.p: Who was it that transported the maiden's chamber, that once stood in the celestial palace, from Olympus to Ephesus the city of Androclus, the queen of the Ionians, swift in battle, most excellent in war and letters? Was it thyself, slayer of Tityus, who, loving thy nurseAccording to one story Artemis was born, not at Delos, but at a place called Ortygia near Ephesus. 1 more than Olympus, didst set thy chamber in her?

div.head: 791.—APOLLONIDES
div.docAuthor: On a Temple of Aphrodite built in the Sea
div.p: Cytherea, who hast established in the depths of the flood the foundations of the sanctuary encinctured by thy mother the sea, around thee the sea rejoices, its blue surface smiling gently under the breeze of Zephyr. Because of this act of piety, and thy temple which Postumus erected, thou shalt boast thee more than because of Paphos.

div.head: 792.—ANTIPATER
div.docAuthor: On the Picture of Ulysses' descent to Hell
div.p: This is the work of Nicias. I am painted here an ever-living City of the dead, the tomb of every age. It was Homer who explored the house of Hades, and I am copied from him as my first original.

div.head: 793.—JULIAN, PREFECT OF EGYPT
div.p: LOOKING on this heifer of Myron's you are like to cry out: "Either Nature is lifeless, or Art is alive."

div.head: 794.—BY THE SAME
div.p: NEAT-HERD, whither dost thou force me to advance? Stop from goading me. Art did not bestow motion on me too.

div.head: 795.—BY THE SAME
div.p: SKILLED Myron either made the bronze alive or drove off a live heifer from the herd and made it into bronze.

div.head: 796.—BY THE SAME
div.p: SCULPTOR Myron, a traveller came to drive off thy heifer, and feeling the bronze turned out to be a futile thief.

div.head: 797.—BY THE SAME
div.p: A LION when he sees me opens his mouth wide, the husbandman picks up his yoke and the herd his staff.

div.head: 798.—BY THE SAME
div.p: BEAR with it, Myron : Art is too strong for thee : the work is lifeless. Art is the child of Nature, for Art did not invent Nature.

div.head: 799.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Porphyry Column in the PhiladelphiaA place so called because the statues of the sons of Constantine the Great stood there.
div.p: MUSELIUS is a well-wisher of the Emperor. Public works proclaim it ; the force of facts is strong. He presented Constantinople with a Museum and with a splendid painting of the sovereign inside, an honour to poets, an ornament of the city, the hope of youth, the instrument of virtue, the wealth of good men.

div.head: 800.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THESE works did Muselius cheerfully dedicate to wordsLiterature.,² in pure belief that God is the Word.

div.head: 801.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: HE built parts of the Museum himself, and other parts which were in danger of falling he saved and set them up firmly.

div.head: 802.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Portrait of the Emperor Marcian
div.p: Thou seest this shape, like a live horse, carrying Marcian, ruler of the race of men. His right hand is outstretched and he spurs on the galloping horse above a foeman, who seems to support its weight on his head.

div.head: 803.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Portrait of the Empress Sophia at the Entrance of the Bath Zeuxippus
div.p: Julian, the prefect of the city, dedicated here Sophia (Wisdom), the queen of the Italians, as being herself full of wisdom.

div.head: 804.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Column with a Statue of the Emperor Justin
div.p: Julian the prefect dutifully set up here the statue of Justin his master and benefactor.

div.head: 805.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Stele of Ares partly buried in Thrace
div.p: As long as this fierce Ares rests on the ground the peoples of the Goths shall never set foot in Thrace.

div.head: 806.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: This place was once a garden, and the shade of the leaves shutting out the sun made it like night.

div.head: 807.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: But now Sergius, the patriarch, who hath seen with his eyes and reveals the mysteries of the Holy Trinity, contrived to make it bright and sunlit. Here this fixed stone seven timesSeemingly this means " by seven lines dividing the dial into six equal parts." 1 announces the eternal and fixed revolutions of the vault of heaven. THE mechanic art compels Phaethon by means of dials ruled in due measure to direct aright (?) the course of the sun. A small stone governs the circle of Aurora by its skilled division into hours and by the shadow's mark. This work of mortals was constructed by the heavenly command of Sergius the patriarch.

div.head: 808.—CYRUS THE CONSUL
div.p: MAXIMINUS built me in the newly constructed Rome, fixing my secure foundations actually on the beach. Infinite beauty extends itself around me. To right, left, and behind me lies the city, but facing me I see all the beauties of the Bithynian coast. At the foot of my most strong foundations the salt current rolls to the lovely sea, just touching the land in front of me enough to wet its edge. Often a man leaning out from me slightly has greatly rejoiced his heart, seeing in all directions different things: trees, houses, ships, sea, city, sky, and earth.

div.head: 809.—BY THE SAME
div.p: Cyrus set up charming Pindar beside the water, because singing to the lyre he said, " Water is best."¹

div.head: 810.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THIS is Justin next Sophia. Both made the golden work after their Assyrian triumph.The Persian war, which, after all, was not very successful.

div.head: 811.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: JUSTINIAN, the emperor, built me the bright house, a marvel for the sun to view at his rising. For never before when he mounted his celestial path did he see such beauty on earth.

div.head: 812.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: DOMNINUS in the pure portals of Justice erected the statue of divine Justin, the pure guardian of Law.

div.head: 813.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: THIS statue of Sophia stands before the gates of Justice, for wisdom should not be apart from justice.

div.head: 814.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: NAIAD Nymphs, ye truants, I never thought you would all quit my streams. But if the bath possesses such charm, Envy will accomplish naught, even though the Nymphs desert all the water.The spring supplying the bath had failed. It is difficult to see how, as the epigram implies, the bath could retain its charm in the absence of water.

div.head: 815.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: STRANGER, why dost thou quicken thy steps now, when thou seest the water that cures pain? This is the bath of joy; it washes away care, it lightens labour. It was built by Michael, the prefect of the Imperial Palace.

div.head: 816.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Dish belonging to Eubulus
div.p: IN presence of Telemachus and near Penelope, why, wise Odysseus, dost thou stretch out thy hand in terror?i.e. signing to the nurse not to reveal who he is. Od. xix. 479. Thy nurse will never tell the suitors of thy gesture.

div.head: 817.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: ON the table of the immaculate sacrifice I depict the passions of those sacrificed for Christ. For those whom I beg to have as protectors have I, Peter, put in the covering of the dread place.

div.head: 818.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I, ANOTHER Peter, not having survived to see the life-giving tomb of the Lord, carved this disc representing the Holy Sepulchre, in which, bending low, I see Christ's body.

div.head: 819.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: I, THE mystic cup, by the flow of the Holy Spirit pour into the heart a stream of repentance.

div.head: 820.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On the Entrance of the HeraeumOn the Asiatic bank of the Bosporus. It is described by Gibbon, chap. xl. Nos. 663 and 664 above may refer to its gardens. ¹
div.p: JUSTINIAN built this magnificent house, a thing of beauty to overhang land and water.

div.head: 821.—ANONYMOUS
div.p: PRINCES, Time will always proclaim your virtue, power, and great deeds, as long as the stars move in heaven.

div.head: 822.—ANONYMOUS
div.docAuthor: On a Dish with the Twelve Signs of the Zodiac
div.p: THIS is the silver heaven where the Moon gazes on the Sun, full herself of his reflected splendour,

div.head: 823.—PLATO
div.p: Let the cliff clothed in greenery of the Dryads keep silence, and the fountains that fall from the rock, and the confused bleating of the ewes newly lambed; for Pan himself plays on his sweet-toned pipe, running his pliant lips over the joined reeds, and around with their fresh feet they have started the dance, the Nymphs, Hydriads, and Hamadryads.

div.head: 824.—ERYCIUS
div.p: Hunters, who come to this peak where dwells mountain Pan, good luck to you in the chase, whether ye go on your way trusting in nets or in the steel, or whether ye be fowlers relying on your hidden limed reeds. Let each of you call on me. I have skill to bring success to trap, spear, nets, and reeds.

div.head: 825.—ANONYMOUS
div.p:
On a Machine for drawing Water which worked noiselessly, on which stood an image of Pan
Echo fled from the waters, too, to escape me, Pan, her unhappy lover.

div.head: 826.—PLATO
div.p:
On a Satyr standing by a Well and Love Asleep
A cunning master wrought me, the Satyr, son of Bacchus, divinely inspiring the monolith with breath. I am the playmate of the Nymphs, and instead of purple wine I now pour forth pleasant water. Guide thy steps here in silence, lest thou disturb the boy lapped in soft sleep.

div.head: 827.—AMMONIUS
div.p: I am the dear servant of horned Dionysus, and pour forth the water of the silver Naiads, soothing the young boy who rests asleep . . .
